A Diagrammatic Axiomatisation of Behavioural Distance of Nondeterministic Processes
Wojciech Różowski, Robin Piedeleu, Alexandra Silva, Fabio Zanasi

Abstract
Behavioural distances provide a quantitative approach to comparing the states of transition systems, moving beyond traditional Boolean notions of equivalence. In this paper, we develop a sound and complete axiomatisation of behavioural distance for nondeterministic processes using Milner’s charts, a model that generalises finite-state automata by incorporating variable outputs. Charts provide a compelling setting for studying behavioural distances because they shift the focus from language equivalence to bisimilarity. Their axiomatic study lays the groundwork for quantitative analysis of more expressive models, such as weighted transition systems. To formalise this approach, we adopt string diagrams as our syntax of choice. String diagrams closely mirror the graphical structure of charts, while providing a rigorous formalism that supports inductive reasoning and compositional semantics. Unlike traditional algebraic syntaxes, which require additional mechanisms such as binders and substitution, string diagrams offer a variable-free representation where recursion naturally decomposes into simpler components. This makes them well-suited for reasoning about behavioural distances and aligns with broader efforts to axiomatise automata-theoretic equivalences through a unified diagrammatic framework.

1
Introduction

In Theoretical Computer Science, it is customary to model computations as transition systems. To facilitate formal analysis of such models, considerable effort has been devoted to developing expressive syntaxes
and compositional reasoning techniques. Notable examples include Kleene algebra
[
30
]
and its extensions
[
21
,
2
,
54
]
, as well as a vast body of work on process calculi
[
35
,
8
,
53
]
. A particularly important feature of such approaches is the presence of an
axiomatisation
—a set of equations that relate syntactic terms that represent semantically equivalent behaviours. When an axiomatisation is available, one may reason about model behaviour via syntactic manipulation of terms, which is particularly well-suited for implementation and automation.

In many contexts, especially when dealing with probabilistic or quantitative models, focussing on exact equivalence of behaviours is too restrictive. Instead, it is often more meaningful to measure how far apart the behaviours of two terms are. This has motivated the development of
behavioural distances
, which endow the state-spaces of transition systems with (pseudo)metric structures quantifying the dissimilarity of states
[
51
,
15
,
7
]
, and
quantitative equational theories

[
33
,
36
]
, which replace equational judgements
s=t
between terms with quantitative ones of the form
s=_{\varepsilon}t
capturing “the distance between
s
and
t
is at most
\varepsilon
”.

Behavioural distances have mostly been studied for probabilistic systems
[
15
,
51
]
. More recently, there has been growing interest in understanding distances in a general categorical framework and how this would yield coarser notions of equivalence for a variety of systems
[
7
]
. The instantiations of that framework, and in particular axiomatisations of distances, are largely unexplored, with the exception of one for deterministic automata
[
42
]
.

In this paper, we take a step further and investigate axiomatisations of behavioural distance for a
nondeterministic
model of computation, known as
charts

[
35
]
. Originally introduced by Milner, charts extend
finite-state nondeterministic automata
(NFA) by replacing the notion of acceptance with variable outputs. Intuitively, the distance between two charts can be quantified by, roughly, the number of steps after which their behaviours disagree—
i.e.
are no longer bisimilar. This seemingly small generalisation from deterministic finite automata provides a range of challenges, stemming from the fact that the presence of non-determinism moves the semantics from language to bisimilarity, while at the same time representing a crucial step towards weighted transition systems
[
31
]
, where the general theory of behavioral distances and axiomatisations thereof is relatively underexplored.

The central contribution of this paper is an inference system for reasoning about behavioural distances of behaviours of Milner’s charts. We demonstrate its
soundness
(
\Cref
thm:soundness) and
completeness
(
\Cref
thm:completeness). On the way, we gather several contributions of independent interest. First, we instantiate the abstract framework of behavioural distances in the concrete case of charts. We organise such behaviours as a symmetric monoidal category, in which they may be composed
sequentially
and
in parallel
. We do so relying on rich structures associated with charts, such as Conway Theories
[
10
,
17
]
. Second, as one of the steps in the soundness argument, we give a concrete characterisation of behavioural distance between charts via Hennessy and Milner’s stratification of bisimilarity
[
24
]
. Finally, the completeness argument makes use of tools from fixpoint theory to simplify the calculation of behavioural distance to the point it can be mimicked via syntactic manipulation.

The syntax and equations of our complete axiomatic theory are given in terms of
string diagrams
, the two-dimensional language of monoidal categories
[
45
,
41
]
. The pictorial representation of string diagrams provides an intuitive understanding of how information flows and is exchanged between components within a system. For this reason, they have been increasingly popular as a formal language for computations and processes in areas such as quantum theory
[
13
]
, concurrency
[
11
]
, probabilistic programming
[
39
]
, and digital circuits
[
18
]
.

a
b
b
a
a
b
a
a
b
a
b
a
a
\equiv_{1/4}
b
a
a
a
a
\big\Uparrow
\big\Downarrow
completeness
,
\mathsf{d}\Bigg(
\Bigg)\leq\frac{1}{4}
soundness

Figure 1:
Two charts at distance
\frac{1}{4}
and their corresponding representations as string diagrams. In Milner’s syntax, the chart on the left can be presented as
a.(a.0+b.\mu v_{1}.a.v_{1})+b.\mu v_{1}.a.v_{1}
, while the chart on the right corresponds to
\mu v_{2}.(a.v_{2}+b.\mu v_{1}.a.a.v_{1})
.

There are several reasons to favour string diagrams as our syntax of choice.
First, they closely resemble the usual graphical representation of the transition structure of charts, while constituting a formal syntax that supports inductive reasoning and to which we can assign semantics formally.
Moreover, as Milner observed
[
35
]
, the standard algebraic syntax of regular expressions is not expressive enough to capture all chart behaviour
[
20
]
. His solution introduced a more complex syntax with binders and names, later studied in the process algebra community for various models, including probabilistic
[
49
]
and quantitative
[
26
]
ones. In contrast, string diagrams offer a variable-free approach, eliminating the need to define substitution and recursion as a primitive operation (the latter is decomposed into simpler components).
Finally, using string diagrams aligns our work with a broader research programme aimed at axiomatising various notions of equivalence in automata theory through a unified diagrammatic syntax
[
40
,
3
]
.

Outline.
In
\Cref
sec:operations, we introduce charts, as well as their associated notions of behavioural equivalence and distances. Then, in
\Cref
sec:syntax, we introduce the syntax of our diagrammatic calculus, for which we construct the semantics in
\Cref
sec:semantics. Next, in
\Cref
sec:axioms we present a (quantitative) equational inference system for reasoning about distances of the denotations of the terms of our calculus; we also prove its soundness and study one example in more detail.
\Cref
sec:completeness contains the main technical result of the paper, namely completeness for the proposed behavioural distance between charts. We wrap up in
\Cref
sec:discussion where we review related literature, and sketch directions for future work.

2
Preliminaries

In this section, we briefly review Milner’s charts
[
35
]
, whose behaviours are the central semantic object of this paper. Then, we instantiate the abstract framework of coalgebraic behavioural metrics
[
7
]
to the concrete case of charts.

(Pre)charts and their algebraic operations.
Fix a set
V=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots\}
of
variables
and
\Sigma
of
letters
respectively. A prechart is a triple
(Q,E,D)
, where
Q
is a set of states,
D\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q
a finite labelled transition relation and
E\subseteq Q\times V
is a finite output relation. Precharts can be thought as a generalisation of nondeterministic automata, where instead of acceptance, we deal with the notion of outputs.
Given a
q\in Q
, we will often write
D(q)=\{(a,q^{\prime})\mid(q,a,q^{\prime})\in D\}
and
E(q)=\{v\mid(q,v)\in E\}
. Moreover, when
D
and
E
are clear from the context, we will write
q\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}q^{\prime}\iff(q,a,q^{\prime})\in D
and
q\rhd v\iff(q,v)\in E
. A chart
C
is a quadruple
(Q,s,D,E)
, where
(Q,D,E)
is a prechart and
s\in Q
is a distinguished start node. We call a chart finite if
Q
is finite. There are several operations on charts that will be of interest in this paper.

•

Empty chart.
We set
0:=(\{s\},s,\emptyset,\emptyset)
.

•

Variable.
Given
v\in V
, we define
v:=(\{s\},s,\emptyset,\{(s,v)\})
.

•

Prefix.
Let
C=(Q,s,D,E)
be a chart and
a\in\Sigma
. We define
a.C:=(Q\cup\{s^{\prime}\},s^{\prime},D\cup\{(s^{\prime},a,s)\},E)
, where
s^{\prime}\notin Q
.

•

Nondeterministic choice.
Let
C_{i}=(Q_{i},s_{i},D_{i},E_{i})
,
i\in\{1,2\}
. For simplicity of presentation, we assume
Q_{1},Q_{2}
to be disjoint and
s\notin Q_{1}\cup Q_{2}
. We define

C_{1}+C_{2}:=(Q_{1}\cup Q_{2}\cup\{s\},s,D_{1}\cup D_{2}\cup D^{\prime},E_{1}\cup E_{2}\cup E^{\prime})

where

D^{\prime}:=\{s\}\times(D_{1}(s_{1})\cup D_{2}(s_{2}))
and
E^{\prime}:=\{s\}\times(E_{1}(s_{1})\cup E_{2}(s_{2}))
.

•

Substitution.
Let
\vec{C}=(C_{1},\dots,C_{n})
and
C
be disjoint charts, and let
\vec{v}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})
be distinct variables. We define

C[\vec{C}/\vec{v}]=\left(Q\cup\bigcup_{i}Q_{i},\{s\},D^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{i}D_{i},E^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{i}E_{i}\right)

where for
q\in Q_{i}
,
D^{\prime}(q)=E^{\prime}(q)=\emptyset
, while for
q\in Q
,

D^{\prime}(q)=D(q)\cup\bigcup_{i}\left\{D_{i}(s_{i})\mid v_{i}\in E(q)\right\}

and

E^{\prime}(q)=(E(q)\setminus\vec{v})\cup\bigcup_{i}\left\{E_{i}(s_{i})\mid v_{i}\in E(q)\right\}
.

•

Recursion.
If
C=(Q,s,D,E)
, then we define
\mu v.C:=(Q,s,D^{+},E^{+})
, where

\displaystyle D^{+}(q)=\begin{cases}D(q)\cup D(s)&\text{if }v\in E(q)\\
D(q)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\qquad E^{+}(q)=\begin{cases}\left(E(q)\cup E(s)\right)\setminus\{v\}&\text{if }v\in E(q)\\
E(q)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

When applied to finite charts, the operations above preserve finiteness. Given a chart
C=(Q,s,D,E)
we say that a variable
v\in V
is
live
in
C
if there exists a path of transitions
s\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a_{1}}$
}\!}\dots\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a_{n}}$
}\!}s^{\prime}\rhd v
or call it
dead
otherwise.
The canonical notion of (pre)charts having the same observational behaviour is given through the following concept.

Definition 1

(Strong Bisimulation)
.

Let
C_{i}=(Q_{i},D_{i},E_{i})
,
i\in\{1,2\}
be precharts. A bisimulation between
C_{1}
and
C_{2}
is a relation
{R}\subseteq Q_{1}\times Q_{2}
, such that
1
if
(q_{1},q_{2})\in R
, then
E(q_{1})=E(q_{2})
,
2
if
(q_{1},q_{2})\in R
and
q_{1}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}q^{\prime}_{1}
, then there exists
q^{\prime}_{2}\in Q_{2}
, such that
q_{2}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}q^{\prime}_{2}
and
(q^{\prime}_{1},q^{\prime}_{2})\in R
and symmetrically. If
C_{1}
and
C_{2}
are charts, we say that they are bisimilar (denoted
C_{1}\sim C_{2}
) if there exists a bisimulation between their underlying precharts that relates their start nodes.

It immediately follows that
\sim
is an equivalence relation on the set of finite charts. We call this relation
bisimilarity
and we will write
\Omega
for the set of all finite charts modulo bisimilarity. We will refer to the elements of this set as
regular behaviours
. Conveniently,
\sim
is a congruence with respect to all operations described above and hence one can unambiguously extend all the mentioned operations to elements of
\Omega

[
35
, Proposition 3.2]
. Let
[C_{1}],[C_{2}]\in\Omega
, such that
C_{1}=(Q,s,D,E)
and
C_{2}=(Q,s^{\prime},D,E)
. One can make
\Omega
into prechart itself by setting
[C_{1}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}[C_{2}]\iff s\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}_{C_{1}}s^{\prime}
and
[C_{1}]\rhd v\iff s\rhd_{C_{1}}v
.

Definition 2

(Prechart homomorphism)
.

Let
C_{i}=(Q_{i},D_{i},E_{i})
,
i\in\{1,2\}
be precharts. We call a function
f\colon Q_{1}\to Q_{2}
a prechart homomorphism if the graph of
f
, given by
G(f)=\{(q,f(q))\mid q\in Q_{1}\}
is a bisimulation between
C_{1}
and
C_{2}
.

Fix a prechart
C=(Q,D,E)
. A map taking each state
s\in Q
to the equivalence class
[(Q,s,D,E)]
in
\Omega
is a homomorphism from
C
into prechart on
\Omega
. It can be easily observed that bisimulations and homomorphisms preserve the liveness of variables. From now on, we will abuse the notation and omit the quotient brackets when talking about elements of
\Omega
.

Pseudometric spaces.
We will formally give the notion of distance between regular behaviours by equipping them with a
pseudometric
structure, a mild generalisation of metric spaces, where we drop the requirement of points in zero distance having to be strictly equal. This stems from the fact that in precharts we might have two states with identical behaviour (and hence zero distance), which are not strictly equal (but rather bisimilar).

Definition 3
.

A 1-bounded pseudometric space is a pair
(X,d_{X})
, where
X
is a set and
d_{X}\colon X\times X\to[0,1]
is a function satisfying
1

d_{X}(x,x)=0
(Reflexivity),
2

d_{X}(x,y)=d_{X}(y,x)
(Symmetry) and
3

d_{X}(x,z)\leq d_{X}(x,y)+d_{X}(y,z)
(Transitivity) for all
x,y,z\in X
.

In this paper, all pseudometric spaces are 1-bounded, and hence we will abuse the terminology and simply call them pseudometric spaces. We call a function
f\colon X\to Y
between pseudometric spaces
(X,d_{X})
and
(Y,d_{Y})
nonexpansive, if
d_{Y}(f(x),f(y))\leq d_{X}(x,y)
for all
x,y\in X
. It is called an isometry if it satisfies
d_{Y}(f(x),f(y))=d_{X}(x,y)
. Given two pseudometric spaces
(X,d_{X})
and
(Y,d_{Y})
one can define their product to be
(X,d_{X})\times(Y,d_{Y})=(X\times Y,d_{X\times Y})
, where
d_{X\times Y}((x,y),(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}))=\max\{d(x,x^{\prime}),d(y,y^{\prime})\}
for all
x,x^{\prime}\in X
and
y,y^{\prime}\in Y
. This can be easily extended to any
n
-tuple. We define
0
-tuples to be given by
1_{\bullet}=(\{\bullet\},d_{\bullet})
, the unique single point pseudometric space, where
d_{\bullet}(\bullet,\bullet)=0
. Given a function of multiple arguments, i.e.
X_{1}\to X_{2}\to Y
, we will call it nonexpansive, if it is nonexpansive as a function
f\colon(X_{1},d_{X_{1}})\times(X_{2},d_{X_{2}})\to(Y,d_{Y})
. Given a set
X
, we write
D_{X}
for the set of all pseudometrics on the set
X
. This set carries a partial order structure, given by
d\sqsubseteq d^{\prime}\iff\forall_{x,x^{\prime}\in X}~d(x,x^{\prime})\leq d^{\prime}(x,x^{\prime})
. For any
X
,
(D_{X},\sqsubseteq)
is a complete lattice
[
7
, Lemma 3.2]
, where supremas can be calculated pointwise. The top element of that lattice is given by the discrete pseudometric
\top\colon X\times X\to[0,1]
such that
\top(x,y)=0
if
x=y
, or
\top(x,y)=1
otherwise.

Behavioural distances.
We now have all the ingredients to formalise the concept of how much apart two regular behaviours are. Notation wise, we will write
P_{\text{fin}}(X)
for the set of
finite
subsets of the set
X
. Given a prechart
(Q,E,D)
, we can equivalently see it as a pair
(Q,\beta)
, where
\beta
is a combined transition function
Q\to P_{\text{fin}}(\Sigma\times Q+V)
taking each state
q\in Q
, to the set
\beta(q)=D(q)\cup E(q)
of possible successors, that include labelled transitions and variable outputs. Given a pseudometric space defined on a state-space of a prechart, we can
lift
it to the set of possible transitions through the following construction.

Definition 4

(Transitions lifting)
.

Let
(X,d)
be a pseudometric space. We write
d^{\uparrow}
for the pseudometric on
\Sigma\times X+V
defined by
d^{\uparrow}(m,n)=\frac{1}{2}d(x,y)
if
m=(a,x)
and
n=(a,y)
,
d^{\uparrow}(m,n)=0
if
m=n
or
d^{\uparrow}(m,n)=1
otherwise.

Similarly, we can lift distances over
X
to distances between elements of
P_{\text{fin}}(X)
.

Definition 5

(Hausdorff lifting)
.

Let
(X,d)
be a pseudometric space. We can equip
P_{\text{fin}}(X)
with a distance function
\mathcal{H}(d)(X,Y)=\max\{\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{y\in Y}d(x,y),\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}d(y,x)\}
making
(P_{\text{fin}}(X),\mathcal{H}(d))
into a pseudometric.

Given a prechart
(Q,\beta)
, whose state-space is equipped with a pseudometric
d_{Q}
, we can define a new pseudometric
\Phi_{\beta}(d_{Q})
that calculates the distance between any pair
q_{1},q_{2}\in Q
of states, by lifting
d_{Q}
to the set
P_{\text{fin}}(\Sigma\times Q+V)
and comparing
\beta(q_{1})
with
\beta(q_{2})
, namely

\Phi_{\beta}(d_{Q})(q_{1},q_{2})=\mathcal{H}\left(d_{Q}^{\uparrow}\right)(\beta(q_{1}),\beta(q_{2}))
. This is used to define the
behavioural distance
.

Theorem 6
.

Let
(Q,\beta)
be a prechart. Then, the following properties hold:
1

d_{Q}\mapsto\Phi_{\beta}(d_{Q})
is a monotone mapping on the lattice
D_{Q}
,
2

\Phi_{\beta}
has a least fixpoint
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}
,
3

x\sim y\implies\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=0
and
4
a homomorphism
f\colon Q\to R
between precharts
(Q,\beta)
and
(R,\gamma)
is an isometry between
(Q,\mathsf{bd}_{\beta})
and
(R,\mathsf{bd}_{\gamma})
.

The theorem above allows one to define a distance between regular behaviours, by calculating the distance in the prechart structure on
\Omega
. We will simply refer to this distance as the
behavioural distance
and denote it by
\mathsf{bd}
. Since prechart homomorphisms are isometries, given two finite charts
C_{1}
and
C_{2}
, their distance is given by
\mathsf{bd}([C_{1}],[C_{2}])
, the distance between their corresponding regular behaviours. Such distance can be characterised concretely via Hennessy and Milner’s
stratification of bisimilarity

[
24
]
.

Definition 7

(Stratification of bisimilarity)
.

Let
C_{i}=(Q_{i},D_{i},E_{i})
for
i\in\{1,2\}
be precharts. We can define a family
\{\sim^{(n)}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
of equivalence relations on
Q_{1}\times Q_{2}
given by the following. For all
(q_{1},q_{2})\in Q_{1}\times Q_{2}
, we have that
q_{1}\sim^{(0)}q_{2}
. Given
(q_{1},q_{2})\in Q_{1}\times Q_{2}
, we have that
q_{1}\sim^{(n+1)}q_{2}
if
1

E_{1}(q_{1})=E_{2}(q_{2})
,
2

q_{1}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}_{C_{1}}q^{\prime}_{1}
implies that there exists
q^{\prime}_{2}\in Q_{2}
, such that
q_{2}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}q^{\prime}_{2}
and
q^{\prime}_{1}\sim^{(n)}q^{\prime}_{2}
and symmetrically.

We can now formally state the correspondence between behavioural distance and stratification of bisimilarity.

Theorem 8
.

Let
C_{i}=(Q_{i},s_{i},D_{i},E_{i})
for
i=\{1,2\}
be finite charts. We have that
\mathsf{bd}([C_{1}],[C_{2}])=0
if
s_{1}\sim s_{2}
. Otherwise,
\mathsf{bd}([C_{1}],[C_{2}])=2^{-n}
, where
n\in\mathbb{N}
is the largest such that
s_{1}\sim^{(n)}s_{2}
.

3
Monoidal Syntax

We adopt the diagrammatic syntax for NFA that has appeared in a number of previous papers
[
40
,
3
]
.
We refer the reader to Selinger’s classic survey
[
45
]
, or to Piedeleu and Zanasi’s recent text for a more gentle introduction to the language of string diagrams
[
41
]
.

This syntax is formalised as a product and permutation category, or prop, a structure which generalises algebraic theories. Formally, a
prop
is a strict symmetric monoidal category (SMC) whose objects are words over a set of generators and whose monoidal product
\oplus
is given by concatenation.
More specifically, our syntax is the free prop
\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}
over the signature
\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{M})
, given by a set
\mathcal{O}
of generating objects and a set
\mathcal{M}
of generating morphisms
g\mathrel{:}\,v\to w
, with
v,w\in\mathcal{O}^{*}
(we use
\epsilon
to denote the empty word). Morphisms of
\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}
can be combined in two different ways, using the composition operation
(-);(-)\mathrel{:}\,\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}(u,v)\times\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}(v,w)\to\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}(u,w)
or the monoidal product
(-)\oplus(-)\mathrel{:}\,\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}(v_{1},w_{1})\times\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}(v_{2},w_{2})\to\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}(v_{1}v_{2},w_{1}w_{2})
. We also have distinguished constants: identities
\mathrm{id}_{w}\mathrel{:}\,w\to w
, which are the unit for composition, and symmetries
\sigma^{v}_{w}\mathrel{:}\,vw\to wv
, to reorder the letters of a given object. In summary, morphisms of
\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}
can be described as terms of the
(\mathcal{O}^{*},\mathcal{O}^{*})
-sorted syntax generated from the constants
\mathcal{M}+\{\mathrm{id}_{w}:w\in\mathcal{O}^{*}\}+\{\sigma^{v}_{w}:v,w\in\mathcal{O}^{*}\}
using the operations
;
and
\oplus
,
quotiented
by the axioms of SMCs. However, the terms of this syntax are very cumbersome to work with.

We adopt a more convenient way to represent morphisms of
\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}
, using the graphical notation of
string diagrams
. In this view, a morphism
f\mathrel{:}\,v\to w
of
\mathsf{T}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathcal{S}}
is depicted as a
f
-labelled box with a
v
-labelled wire on the left and a
w
-labelled wire on the right. The operations of composition and monoidal product are represented by connecting two boxes horizontally and juxtaposing two boxes vertically, respectively:

f
u
v
g
w
f_{1}
f_{2}
v_{1}
w_{1}
v_{2}
w_{2}

Wires
w
represent identities, the wire crossing
v
w
represents the symmetry
\sigma^{v}_{w}
, and the empty diagram
the identity
\mathrm{id}_{\epsilon}\mathrel{:}\,\epsilon\to\epsilon
.

. We call
inputs
the incoming wires of a diagram, and
outputs
its outgoing wires; formally, the inputs (resp. outputs) of
f\mathrel{:}\,v\to w
are the set of positions of the word
v
which are
\blacktriangleright
(resp.
\blacktriangleleft
) and the position of
w
which are
\blacktriangleleft
(resp.
\blacktriangleright
).

4
Monoidal Semantics

In order to interpret the string diagrams described in
\Cref
sec:syntax, we construct an appropriate semantic universe out of regular behaviours. As much as the technical development makes use of category theory, we will keep the description of the formalism high-level. The fine-grained details are relegated to
\Cref
apx:semantics.
We will write
V_{n}
for the set
V_{n}=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}\subseteq V
and
\Omega(n)
for the set of all regular behaviours whose live variables are contained in the set
V_{n}
. For any
m,n\in\mathbb{N}
, we will write
\mathsf{RegBeh}(n,m)
for the set of
n
-tuples of elements of
\Omega(m)
. There are several operations involving these sets that are of interest:

•

Identity.
For every
n\in\mathbb{N}
, we define
\mathrm{id}_{n}\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(n,n)
as
\mathrm{id}_{n}=\vec{v}_{n}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})
. When
n
is clear from the context, we will abuse the notation and simply write
\vec{v}
instead.

•

Sequential composition.
Given
f\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,n)
and
g\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(n,p)
, we can define their sequential composition
f;g\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,p)
to be given by
(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{v}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{v}])
, where
\vec{v}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})
. The sequential composition is associative, with identity being a neutral element when composed both on the left and right (see
\Cref
lem:comp_associative in the appendix of the full version of the paper).

•

Initial object.
For every
n\in\mathbb{N}
, there is a unique element
0_{n}\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(0,n)
given by the empty tuple.

•

Pairing.
Given
f\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(k,m)
and
g\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(l,m)
, we define their pairing
\langle f,g\rangle\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(k+l,m)
, by setting
\langle f,g\rangle=(f_{1},\dots,f_{k},g_{1},\dots g_{l})
.

•

Parallel composition.
Given
f\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(k,l)
and
g\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,n)
, we can define their parallel composition
f\oplus g\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(k+m,l+n)
, by setting

f\oplus g=(f_{1},\dots,f_{k},g_{1}[(v_{l+1},\dots,v_{l+n})/\vec{v}],\dots,g_{m}[(v_{l+1},\dots,v_{l+n})/\vec{v}])

•

Codiagonal.
For any
n\in\mathbb{N}
, there is a
n+n
-tuple
\nabla_{n}\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(n+n,n)
called codiagonal given by
\nabla_{n}=\langle\mathrm{id}_{n},\mathrm{id}_{n}\rangle
.

•

Dagger.
For any
f\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(1,p+1)
, we can define
f^{\dagger}\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(1,p)
to be given by
f^{\dagger}=\mu v_{p+1}.f
. Following
[
17
, Remark 3.2]
, we can inductively extend the dagger to the map taking each
f\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(n,p+n)
to
f^{\dagger}\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(n,p)
.

Categorical structure.

We now define a category
\mathsf{RegBeh}
, whose objects are natural numbers and morphisms
f\colon m\to n
are elements
f\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,n)
. This category has a rich structure that will be useful when defining the semantics of our diagrammatic language.

Theorem 10
.

The category
\mathsf{RegBeh}
has the following properties:

•

\mathsf{RegBeh}
has all finite coproducts.

•

(\mathsf{RegBeh},\oplus,0)
is a (co-Cartesian) strict symmetric monoidal category.

•

\mathsf{RegBeh}
equipped with a dagger is a Conway theory
[
17
]
.

•

Each morphism
g\colon p+n\to q+n
has a trace
\mathsf{Tr}^{n}_{p,q}(g)\colon p\to q
defined in terms of
(-)^{\dagger}
. This equipment makes
\mathsf{RegBeh}
into a traced monoidal category
[
27
]
.

Pseudometric structure.

\mathsf{RegBeh}
additionally carries a well-behaved pseudometric structure. For all
m,n\in\mathbb{N}
each set
\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,n)
can be made into a pseudometric space by equipping it with a distance function, given by
d^{m,n}((f_{1},\dots,f_{m}),(g_{1},\dots,g_{m}))=\sup_{1\leq i\leq m}\left\{\mathsf{bd}(f_{i},g_{i})\right\}
.
Intuitively, we calculate the distance between
m
-tuples of regular behaviours, by taking the pointwise behavioural distance of elements of tuples and then taking the maximum. In the corner case, when both tuples are empty, then they are simply at distance zero. This equipment satisfies the following property.

Proposition 11
.

Equipping each set
\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,n)
of morphisms of
\mathsf{RegBeh}
with a pseudometric defined above makes a sequential composition, pairing, parallel composition, dagger and trace into nonexpansive maps.

Remark 12
.

Although we do not pursue such a perspective in this paper, a categorically inclined reader may observe that equipping
\mathsf{RegBeh}
with a pseudometric structure yields an enrichment over
\mathsf{PMet}
—the monoidal category of pseudometric spaces with the categorical product as its monoidal product. Since
\mathsf{PMet}
is a concrete category (i.e., it admits a faithful functor to
\mathsf{Set}
), the conditions for enrichment simplify significantly: they reduce to verifying that all the relevant operations (composition, monoidal product, etc.) are nonexpansive on each homset and that the components of the natural transformations that define the monoidal structure are nonexpansive maps, which is exactly what we have shown above. For further details on pseudometric enrichment of monoidal categories and quantitative equational theories, we refer the reader to the recent work of Lobbia et al.
[
32
]
.

Bidirectional maps and loops.
Each morphism
f\colon m\to n
of
\mathsf{RegBeh}
can be informally thought of as a process that has
directionality
to it, i.e. it takes
m
inputs and produces
n
outputs. Informally speaking, the trace operator provides a
global
feedback operation. At the same time, the syntax of our diagrammatic language is
bidirectional
and the notion of feedback is introduced
locally
by bending the wires. To reconcile these points of view, we rely on the
Int
construction
[
27
]
, which takes a traced monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
and completes it into a compact closed category
\mathbf{Int}(\mathcal{C})
, a categorical structure with sequential and parallel composition equipped with duals (allowing to swap directionality) and adjoints (allowing to form local loops representing feedback)
[
28
]
.
\mathbf{Int}(\mathcal{C})
carries the same information as
\mathcal{C}
, but represents it in an alternative, bidirectional way.
We now briefly describe
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
(see
\Cref
sec:apx_int for more detail).

•

The objects of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
are pairs
(m,n)
of natural numbers.

•

A morphism
f\colon(k,l)\to(m,n)
, representing a process with
k
left inputs,
l
left outputs,
m
right outputs and
n
right inputs is a map
f\colon k+m\to l+n
in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
, i.e. we group inputs and outputs together. Composition of
f\colon(k,l)\to(m,n)
and
g\colon(m,n)\to(p,q)
is defined by forming a trace that resolves the feedback involving
m
and
n
.

•

The parallel composition of
f\colon(m,n)\to(p,q)
and
g\colon(m^{\prime},n^{\prime})\to(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})
is given by the map
f\otimes g\colon(m+m^{\prime},n+n^{\prime})\to(p+p^{\prime},q+q^{\prime})
that is defined via parallel composition in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
combined with an appropriate reordering of elements of tuples involved.

•

A dual of the object
(m,n)
of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is given by
(n,m)
. Intuitively, inputs become swapped with outputs. For each object
(m,n)
of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
, there is a unit map
\eta_{(m,n)}\colon(0,0)\to(m+n,m+n)
and counit
\epsilon_{(m,n)}\colon(m+n,m+n)\to(0,0)
. These represent the bending of the wires on the right and left respectively. Following
[
27
]
, one can equip
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
with a trace operator defined in terms of the units and counits.

•

\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
inherits the pseudometric structure from
\mathsf{RegBeh}
, by setting
d^{(k,l),(m,n)}
to be given by
d^{k+n,l+n}
(defined before).

The following theorem intuitively states that on
directional
processes
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is exactly the same as
\mathsf{RegBeh}
.

Theorem 13

(
[
27
, Proposition 5.1]
)
.

There is a full and faithful traced monoidal functor
N\colon\mathsf{RegBeh}\to\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
that takes each
f\colon n\to m
in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
to
f\colon(n,0)\to(m,0)

Moreover, the pseudometric structure interacts well with the operations of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
.

Proposition 14
.

The sequential and parallel composition in
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is nonexpansive. Moreover, the fully faithful functor
N\colon\mathsf{RegBeh}\to\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is locally an isometry, i.e. for all
f,g\colon m\to n
, we have that
d^{m,n}(f,g)=d^{(m,0),(n,0)}(N(f),N(g))
.

Functorial semantics.
We are ready to state the semantics of our diagrammatic language
\left\llbracket{-}\right\rrbracket\colon\mathsf{Syn}\to\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
as a symmetric monoidal functor from
\mathsf{Syn}
to
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
. Since the syntax is a freely generated prop, in order to interpret arbitrary string diagrams it is enough to just define the interpretation of the generating morphisms of
\mathsf{Syn}
. We have:

5
Axiomatisation

Our main aim in this paper is to find a set of (quantitative) equations to reason about semantic distance directly at the level of the diagrams themselves. To do so, we distinguish two different relations on diagrams of the same type:

•

An equational theory intended to capture (strong) bisimilarity of regular behaviours, allowing us to simplify the diagrams whose distance is being compared.

•

A quantitative equational theory intended to capture the behavioural distance of
\Cref
sec:semantics, that is the subject of the completeness theorem (
\Cref
thm:completeness) described in
\Cref
sec:completeness. Note that this theory contains the equational axioms as rules for distance zero.

Equational theory.
Our equational theory is the smallest congruence (w.r.t to vertical and horizontal compositions) that includes the axioms of Fig.
2
. In practice, this means that, if we find a sub-diagram that matches one side of an axiom in a larger diagram, we can replace it with the other side of the axiom (the left and right-hand side of any axiom have the same type)
[
41
, Section 2.1]
.

Figure 2:
Equational axioms for regular behaviours.

Axioms
A1
-
A2
are those of
compact closed categories

[
28
]
and allow us to bend and straighten wires at will, only keeping track of their directions. Crucially, they also allow us to manipulate feedback loops; in Milner’s syntax, they are the structural rules that let one rearrange a system of recursive equations without changing its solution.

B1-B3
encode the fact that
and
form a
cocommutative comonoid
. These guarantee that nondeterministic choice behaves like a commutative, associative and unital operation in our diagrammatic syntax.
B1
corresponds to associativity
t_{1}+(t_{2}+t_{3})=(t_{1}+t_{2})+t_{3}
,
B2
to the right unit law
t+0=t
, and
B3
to commutativity
t_{1}+t_{2}=t_{2}+t_{1}
. At the same time,
B4-B6
are the dual of the previous three, and make
and
into a
commutative monoid
.
These guarantee that output wires behave like the variables of our diagrammatic syntax: read in Milner’s notation,
B4
states that successive merges associate, so that merging
v_{3}
into
v_{2}
and then
v_{2}
into
v_{1}
yields the same result as merging
v_{3}
into
v_{2}
after
v_{2}
has already been merged into
v_{1}
;
B5
states that renaming an empty tuple has no effect; and
B6
states that merging is symmetric in the two variables being identified.

B7
-
B9
make the previous monoid-comonoid pair into a
bimonoid
expressing how nondeterministic choice and variable-merging interact. Concretely,
B7
states that merging two variables and then forming a nondeterministic choice can be expressed as a pair of nondeterministic choices followed by pairwise merging.
B8
says that the merging operation followed by a deadlock is the same as a pair of deadlocked processes, and
B9
says that the empty tuple of processes is itself unchanged by variable merging.
B10
makes nondeterministic choice an idempotent operation
t+t=t
.

Axiom
B11
allows one to remove unguarded loops, capturing the standard equation
\mu v_{1}.v_{1}=0
. Finally,
C1
encodes the fact that merging tuples of variables interacts as expected with prefixing:
(a.v_{1},a.v_{1})=(a.v_{1},a.v_{2}[v_{1}/v_{2}])
. Note that, if we replace the
with
, the resulting equality (prefixes distribute over nondeterministic sum) is not valid, which is precisely the law that fails for bisimilarity, but holds for trace equivalence
[
40
]
.

Lemma 15

(Soundness)
.

For any two diagrams
f,g\mathrel{:}\,v\to w
of
\mathsf{Syn}
, if
f=g
then
\left\llbracket{f}\right\rrbracket=\left\llbracket{g}\right\rrbracket
.

Quantitative theory.
We define
E_{q}
to be the set of triples of the form
(s,\varepsilon,t)
, where
s,t
are string diagrams of the same type and
\varepsilon\in\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
, to be the least set closed under the rules of Fig.
3
. We will call elements of that set
derivable equations
.

Figure 3:
Quantitative axioms for regular behaviours.

For any two diagrams
f,g\mathrel{:}\,v\to w
of
\mathsf{Syn}
, we say a quantitative equation
f\equiv_{\varepsilon}g
is
valid
if
d^{\left\llbracket{v}\right\rrbracket,\left\llbracket{w}\right\rrbracket}(\left\llbracket{f}\right\rrbracket,\left\llbracket{g}\right\rrbracket)\leq\varepsilon
. Analogously, an inference rule is valid if, whenever all quantitative equations in the premise are valid, then the equation in the conclusion in the equation is also valid.

We now briefly explain each of the rules of our inference system depicted on
\Cref
fig:quantitative-axioms.
(Refl)
,
(Sym)
and
(Triang)
respectively capture reflexivity, symmetry and triangle inequality of pseudometric spaces. Importantly, rule
(Refl)
allows one to state that equal diagrams (modulo strictly equational rules described above) are at distance zero of each other.
(Top)
allows us to state that any two diagrams are at most within distance
1
of each other, while
(Max)
allows one to always weaken the bound on the distance at which two diagrams are.
(Cont)
is the key analytic inference rule here: it allows us to conclude that two diagrams are within distance
\varepsilon
, provided we can show that they are within all distances that are strictly greater than
\varepsilon
, thereby passing to the limit.

Next,
(Seq)
and
(Tens)
relate the horizontal and vertical compositions of diagrams to the distance. There are two domain-specific rules that we use.
(Pref)
witnesses the fact that prefixing by the same actions decreases the distance by half.
Note that it applies to diagram
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
and that we use
\vec{a}
m
m
to denote the vertical composition of
m
many
a
generators, for any
m\in\mathbb{N}
. We note that the factor
\frac{1}{2}
used in
\Cref
def:edge can be replaced with arbitrary real number
k\in\mathopen{[}0,1\mathclose{]}
, but this would require appropriately changing the rule
(Pref)
, as it is the case in the quantitative axiomatisation of the behavioural distance of DFA
[
42
]
. Finally,
(Codel)
axiom encodes that any diagram with no initial state has no behaviour and is therefore at distance zero of the empty chart.

Through a straightforward structural induction, one can show the soundness of the proposed quantitative rules.

Theorem 16

(Quantitative soundness)
.

Every derivable equation
f\equiv_{\varepsilon}g
is valid.

Example 17
.

We revisit the charts from
\Cref
fig:intro, which in Milner’s syntax read
a.(a.0+b.\mu v_{1}.a.v_{1})+b.\mu v_{1}.a.v_{1}
on the left and
\mu v_{2}.(a.v_{2}+b.\mu v_{1}.a.a.v_{1})
on the right. We show that their distance is bounded by
\frac{1}{4}
, which is the same as showing that they agree up to depth of two. The derivation below shows how this bound is obtained
syntactically
, by manipulating the diagrammatic representations through the rules of our inference system. We use compositionality to our advantage and break them into two parts which we will compose later with the
(Comp)
rule. In
1
, we show that
a.(a.0+b.v_{1})+b.v_{1}
and
\mu v_{2}.(a.v_{2}+b.v_{1})
are in distance
\frac{1}{4}
. It is the case, as both processes can be distinguished at the depth of three; in particular, taking three successive
a
-transitions is possible in the right diagram, while in the left one, one reaches a deadlock after two
a
-transitions. In the proof, we use
(Pref)
rule twice, as we show that we agree for all prefixes of the depth of two.

1

\begin{gathered}\frac{\frac{\frac{\frac{\frac{\frac{\frac{}{{\ignorespaces}\ignorespaces{\ignorespaces}\ignorespaces\hbox to30.45pt{\vbox to5.2pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 17.06271pt\lower-2.59998pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{

In the rules labelled with
(\mathsf{Refl};\mathsf{Triang})
we have used the strict equality of diagrams to simplify the quantitative equations. The equalities marked with
(Unroll)
follow from
\Cref
lem:unroll, which we state in the next section. Then, for the second part of our diagrams, we show that
\mu v_{1}.a.v_{1}
is bisimilar to
\mu v_{1}.a.a.v_{1}
. In
2
, we first show that we can easily conclude that both diagrams are in a distance bounded by
\frac{1}{2}
.

6
Completeness

We finally arrive at the main technical section of the paper, where we gradually present a sequence of results leading to the completeness of our axioms for the behavioural distance. First, we show that we can safely focus solely on
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagrams. Then, through an analytic proof relying on
(Cont)
rule, we show that each diagram can be
co-copied
. Consequently, we can decompose any
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagram into a collection of
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagrams, which correspond to individual charts. We argue that each of those
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagrams has a normal form from which one can extract a finite prechart structure. The distance between states of this prechart precisely captures the distance between the diagrams being related and very importantly, admits a simple characterisation that can be simulated through the inference rules of our system, eventually leading to the completeness result.

Left-to-right diagrams.
The following result allows us to turn any bidirectional diagram into a left-to-right one by appropriately
bending
the wires using
and
. We will see later that this process does not change distances between diagrams.

Lemma 18
.

There are bijections between the sets
\mathsf{Syn}(v_{1}\!\blacktriangleleft\!v_{2},w)
and
\mathsf{Syn}(v_{1}v_{2},w\!\blacktriangleright)
, and between
\mathsf{Syn}(v,w_{1}\!\blacktriangleleft\!w_{2})
and
\mathsf{Syn}(v\!\blacktriangleright,w_{1}w_{2})
,
i.e.
between sets of string diagrams of the form

v_{1}
w
v_{2}

and

v_{1}
w
v_{2}

as well as between

w_{1}
v
w_{2}

and

w_{1}
v
w_{2}

where
v,w,v_{i},w_{i}
are words over
\{\blacktriangleright,\blacktriangleleft\}
.

A
block
is simply a diagram freely composed from a restricted set of generators (possibly including identities and symmetries). In this paper, we will make use of two special kinds of diagrams that can be factored into blocks:

•

A
matrix-diagram
is a diagram
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
that factors as a composition of a block of

. A matrix-diagram is
guarded
when any path from left to right port encounters at least one
a
. In
\Cref
lem:guarded-precompose in the appendix of the full version of the paper, we show that one can generalise
(Pref)
inference rule to arbitrary guarded matrix-diagrams, rather than just vectors of
a
. In other words, prepending a guarded matrix-diagram to any pair of diagrams contracts the distance between them.

•

relation-diagram
is a diagram

Intuitively, matrix-diagrams are representations of labelled transition relations, while relation-transition diagrams are representations of the output relations. This idea can be captured formally through the notion of a
representation
. For a diagram
d\mathrel{:}\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
, a
representation
is a pair
(a,o)
of a guarded matrix-diagram
c\mathrel{:}\,\blacktriangleright^{\ell+m}\to\blacktriangleright^{\ell+m}
and a relation-diagram
o\mathrel{:}\,\blacktriangleright^{\ell+m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
, such that

d
n
m

=

o
c^{*}
\ell
\ell
n
m

:=

\ell
o
c
n
m

(1)

Using the rules of
{=}
, we can rearrange the any diagram into the form described above.

Theorem 19
.

Any diagram
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
has a representation.

The matrix-diagram in the representation that is being fed through feedback, can be
unrolled
.

.

d\mathrel{:}\,\blacktriangleright^{n}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}

.

We informally state the following connection between representations and charts.

Remark 21
.

The diagrammatic syntax presented in our paper is
expressive
, that is, the semantics of every chart can be equivalently encoded as an appropriate diagram. More explicitly, to encode a chart
(Q,s,D,E)
we first define its transition relation
D
as a matrix-diagram
c
and its outputs
E
as a relation diagram
o
; we then compose them together as in (
1
) following the definition of representations above. Semantically, this corresponds to taking a dagger (
\Cref
lem:regbehconway), which solves the system of equations (described by
c
and
o
) using
\mu
operation on charts, recovering the original expressivity result for Milner’s operations on finite charts
[
35
, Corollary 5.8]
, as summarised in
\Cref
sec:operations. Co-deleting all input wires except the one corresponding to the initial state
s\in Q
, yields a diagram whose semantics coincides precisely with the semantics of the chart of interest.

Co-copying.
Bringing each diagram to a form corresponding to its representation, combined with the usage of unrolling (
\Cref
lem:unroll) and generalisation of
(Pref)
to guarded matrix-diagrams (
\Cref
lem:guarded-precompose) allows to show that the following two diagrams are arbitrarily close and hence by
(Cont)
are in zero distance

Theorem 22
.

For any diagram
d\mathrel{:}\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
, we have that

{\ignorespaces}\ignorespaces{\ignorespaces}\ignorespaces\hbox to71.55pt{\vbox to34.48pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 41.0481pt\lower-17.24164pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{
{
{}{}{}}{}{{}}{}
{
{}{}{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}
{{{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}}{
{}{}{}}{{{}}{{}}}{

A very important consequence of the above combined with the usage of
(Codel)
rule is the fact that each
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagram can be separated to a collection of
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
intuitively corresponding to individual entries of tuples being manipulated in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
.

Moreover, in
\Cref
lem:distance_on_merge in the appendix of the full version of the paper, we show that the behavioural distance between the denotations of arbitrary diagrams
f,g\colon\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
is simply the maximum of the component-wise distances between each
f_{i}
and
g_{i}
for
i\in\{1,\dots,m\}
. From now on, we will temporarily shift focus to
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagrams.

One-to-n diagrams.
Each of the
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagrams represents a behaviour of the single state of the prechart structure on
\Omega
or equivalently, defines a chart. Turns out that appropriately combining these diagrams corresponds to operations on charts described in
\Cref
sec:operations.

.

.

This operation of combining two
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
string diagrams (that we call
convolution
) can easily be extended to any finite collection of
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagrams and is well defined up to permutations and removing duplicates, while staying at distance zero; (see
\Cref
lem:convolution-aci). Thanks to the ability to turn each diagram
f\colon\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
into its representation (
\Cref
thm:representation), as well as global co-copying (
\Cref
lem:injections), we can express each the subdiagrams
f_{i}\colon\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
as convolution.

Lemma 25
.

For any diagram
f\colon\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
and
f_{i}
,
1\leq i\leq m
defined as above, for all
i\in\{1,\dots,m\}
, we can derive

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}{\ignorespaces}\ignorespaces{\ignorespaces}\ignorespaces

where, for
1\leq j\leq\ell
, each
v_{q_{j}}\mathrel{:}\,\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
is a diagram encoding the output variables to which the
i
-th input wire of
f
is directly connected, that is, without going through any
a
generator (in particular, each
v_{q_{j}}
is a monoidal product of a single identity with
n-1

generators).

The informal intuition is that each of the
f_{i}\colon\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagrams represents a state of a prechart and the behaviour of each such state is the union of all possible labelled transitions to other states and variable outputs. This can be made formal, by extracting a prechart over the set
Q_{f}=\{f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\}
, whose transition function
\beta
is given by the following; we define
f_{i}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}f_{j}
iff
f_{i}
n
contains
f_{j}
n
a
and similarly
f_{i}\rhd v_{s}
iff
f_{i}
n
contains
v_{s}
n
. The behavioural distance between states of this prechart, precisely captures the behavioural distance between each of the
f_{i}
diagrams.

Lemma 26
.

For all
f_{i},f_{j}\in Q_{f}
, we have that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(f_{i},f_{j})=\mathsf{bd}(\left\llbracket{f_{i}}\right\rrbracket,\left\llbracket{f_{j}}\right\rrbracket)

Completeness.
The behavioural distance between states of finite charts, including those derived from the normal form of diagrams (
\Cref
lem:fundamental), can be given a simpler characterisation via a decreasing chain of approximants.

Lemma 27
.

Let
(Q,\beta)
be a finite prechart. The behavioural distance between any pair
q_{1},q_{2}\in Q
of states can be calculated by
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(q_{1},q_{2})=\inf_{p\in\mathbb{N}}\left\{\Phi^{(p)}_{\beta}(q_{1},q_{2})\right\}
, where
\Phi^{(0)}_{\beta}
is a discrete pseudometric and for any
p\in\mathbb{N}
, we define
\Phi^{(p+1)}_{\beta}=\Phi_{\beta}\left(\Phi^{(p)}_{\beta}\right)
.

The proof of the fact above makes use of the fact that the map
\Phi_{\beta}
has a
unique fixpoint
and when dealing with finite precharts, we can establish necessary preconditions allowing to use Kleene’s fixpoint theorem for the greatest fixpoint. Details of these arguments can be found in
\Cref
apx:dist. The characterisation described above is particularly useful, as upper bounds on each of the approximants can be derived syntactically through the means of axiomatic manipulation.

solved above. This yields completeness result for left-to-right diagrams.

\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}

and
, while preserving distances between diagrams, we arrive at the desired result.

7
Discussion

In this paper, we presented a sound and complete quantitative axiomatisation of the behavioural distance of Milner’s charts
[
35
]
. We have relied on a compositional, string diagrammatic syntax
[
40
,
3
]
and equipped it with a quantitative inference system for reasoning about bounds on behavioural distance, inspired by recent advances in metric universal algebra
[
33
,
34
,
36
]
.

Originally introduced for probabilistic systems
[
51
,
15
]
, behavioural distances have recently been generalised to a broad range of systems modelled via the abstract framework of universal coalgebra
[
43
]
, leveraging pseudometric liftings of functors
[
7
]
. The notion of behavioural distance for charts used in the paper is an instance of this coalgebraic framework. Our concrete characterisation closely resembles the metric on trees studied by Nivat
[
37
]
. A similar characterisation was studied by Golson and Rounds
[
19
]
, who instead examined de Bakker and Zucker’s metric domain for nondeterministic processes
[
14
]
, also derived via a fixpoint construction involving the Hausdorff distance.

The idea of reasoning about distances between string diagrams has been explored before in quantum theory
[
29
,
12
,
25
]
and probability theory
[
38
]
. However, in contrast with the growing body of work on cartesian quantitive algebra
[
33
,
36
,
6
]
, a systematic foundation to axiomatising distances between string diagrams appeared only very recently, in the work of Lobbia et al
[
32
]
. Besides the basic examples provided in
[
32
]
, our work is the first to propose a complete axiomatisation of a quantitative calculus of string diagrams. The approach of
[
32
]
is based on enriched category theory: similarly, one could observe that the equipment of our semantic category with pseudometric structures making sequential and parallel composition nonexpansive yields the enrichment in the category of pseudometric spaces. However, our axiomatisation relies on the domain-specific implicational rule
(Pref)
and an axiom schema
(Codel)
that cannot be expressed in the framework of Lobbia et al
[
32
]
, which only supports quantitative equations. Reconciling those rule formats with the general framework of Lobbia et al
[
32
]
is an interesting direction for future research.

Axiomatising behavioural distances have been originally studied through ad-hoc inference systems
[
31
,
16
]
. The introduction of quantitative equational theories made more principled approaches possible, leading to axiomatisations of behavioural distance for probabilistic systems
[
4
,
5
]
. In recent work, Różowski
[
42
]
extended these results within a coalgebraic framework, focusing on the simple case of DFA, which enjoys a straightforward algebraic representation via the syntax of Kleene Algebra. While we rely here on the general pattern of the completeness proof from that work, the case of Milner’s charts was significantly more involved, requiring the ability to simulate the behaviour of Hausdorff lifting syntactically.

In constructing the semantic category, we have used the fact that charts form a Conway theory
[
17
]
, studied in the literature on parametrised fixpoint operators
[
22
,
47
,
1
]
, and which can be seen as a relaxation of iteration theories
[
10
]
. The connection between charts and these structures was previously investigated by Bloom et al
[
9
]
and Sewell
[
46
]
, while the interplay of parametrised fixpoint operators with traced monoidal categories was studied by Hasegawa
[
23
]
, Haghverdi
[
22
]
, and Simpson and Plotkin
[
47
]
independently.

Our work constitutes a necessary first step towards a similar diagrammatic treatment of behavioural distance for quantitative automata, such as probabilistic and weighted systems, for which distances are a more suitable way of reasoning rather than Boolean equivalences. The string diagrammatic point of view would enable a desirable, compositional treatment that reflects well the underlying operational models, in a way that is not available through conventional syntaxes. Another promising direction for future work would be to consider Guarded Kleene Algebra with Tests (GKAT)
[
48
,
44
]
, an efficiently decidable language for reasoning about equivalence of uninterpreted programs. The completeness proof of GKAT relies on a metric argument that could be internalised within an inference system like the one introduced in this paper. Moreover, the syntax of GKAT is insufficiently expressive, as it can only describe a part of the behaviours of its underlying operational model – in fact there is no finite purely algebraic syntax that could do so
[
50
]
. A string diagrammatic treatment could allow us to express all such behaviours and obtain a simpler yet more expressive completeness result, that would in turn enable axiomatic reasoning about decompilation algorithms, that were recently shown to be expressible via GKAT automata (but not in GKAT)
[
55
]
.

Appendix A
Appendix

A.1
Algebra of Regular Behaviours

In the appendix, we rely on a slightly different, but equivalent
[
35
]
, characterisation of the set
\Omega
of all regular behaviours. In this section, we elaborate on this characterisation and related conventions. In particular, we will write
{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
instead of
\Omega
, as we will view this set as a bisimilarity quotient of a certain specification language that can be given operational semantics by equipping it with a prechart structure. The syntax of the language corresponds to operations described in
\Cref
sec:operations and is given by the following syntax

e,f\in\mathsf{Exp}::=0\mid v\in V\mid a.e\mid e+f\mid\mu v.e

where
V=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots\}
and
\Sigma
be sets of
variables
and
letters
respectively. Given an expression
f
containing a variable
v
, we say that
v
is
free
in
f
, if it appears outside of the scope of the
\mu v.e
operator or say that it is
bound
otherwise. Given an expression
e\in\mathsf{Exp}
, we write
\mathsf{fv}(e)\subseteq V
for the set of its free variables. Given a set
X
, we define
\mathcal{B}X
to be
P_{\text{fin}}(V+\Sigma\times X)
. Recall that each prechart can be equivalently seen as a pair
(X,\beta\colon X\to\mathcal{B}X)
. Given a prechart
(X,\beta)
, we write
x\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}_{\beta}y\iff(a,y)\in\beta(x)
and
x\rhd_{\beta}v_{i}\iff v_{i}\in\beta(x)
. When
\beta
is obvious from the context, we will omit writing it in the subscript. One can easily verify that
\sim_{\beta}
is a prechart bisimulation itself and we will refer to it as the
greatest bisimulation
on
(X,\beta)
. When
\beta
is obvious from the context we will omit writing it in the subscript.

Definition 32
.

Let
(X,\beta)
be a prechart and let
Y\subseteq X
. We call
(Y,\beta)
a subprechart of
(X,\beta)
, if the canonical inclusion map
i\colon Y\to X
is a prechart homomorphism.

Given a prechart
(X,\beta)
and a state
x
we write
\langle x\rangle_{\beta}\subseteq X
for the set of states reachable from
x
(note that this definition can be easily extended to sets of states). Equipping in with
\beta
restricted to
\langle x\rangle_{\beta}
defines a subprechart
(\langle x\rangle_{\beta},\beta)
of
(X,\beta)
.

Definition 33

(
[
35
]
)
.

Given vectors
\vec{v}
of binders and
\vec{e}
of expressions of the same size, we define a syntactic substitution operator
[\vec{e}/\vec{v}]\colon\mathsf{Exp}\to\mathsf{Exp}
by the following

\displaystyle v[\vec{e}/\vec{v}]=\begin{cases}\vec{e}_{i}&\text{if }v=\vec{v}_{i}\\
v&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\qquad(a.e)[\vec{e}/\vec{v}]=a.(e[\vec{e}/\vec{v}])

\displaystyle(e+f)[\vec{e}/\vec{v}]=e[\vec{e}/\vec{v}]+f[\vec{e}/\vec{v}]

\displaystyle(\mu w.e)[\vec{e}/\vec{v}]=\begin{cases}\mu w.(e[\vec{e}/\vec{v}])&\text{if }w\text{ is not in }\vec{v}\text{ nor free in }\vec{e}\\
\mu w.(e[z/w][\vec{e}/\vec{v}])&\text{otherwise for some }z\text{ not in }\vec{v}\text{ nor free in }\vec{e}\\
\end{cases}

Definition 34

(
[

]

Let
(\mathsf{Exp},\partial)
be a prechart whose transition function (called
derivative
) is a least one satisfying the following inference rules

\displaystyle\frac{e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}e^{\prime}}{a.e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}e^{\prime}}\qquad\frac{}{v\rhd v}\qquad\frac{e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{

$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}e^{\prime}}\qquad\frac{f\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$

$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}f^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\frac{e\rhd v}{e+f\rhd v}\qquad\frac{f\rhd v}{e+f\rhd v}\qquad\frac{e\rhd v\quad v\neq w}{\mu w.e\rhd v}\qquad\frac{e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}e^{\prime}}{\mu v.e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$

The syntactic prechart

is locally finite.

Lemma 41
.

For all
e,f_{1},\dots,f_{m},g_{1},\dots,g_{m}\in\mathsf{Exp}
and vectors
\vec{v}=(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}}),\vec{w}=(v_{j_{1}},\dots,v_{j_{n}})
, such that all free variables of
e
are contained in
\vec{v}
and all free variables of
\vec{f}
are contained in
\vec{w}
, we have that

(e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}])[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]=e[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}])/\vec{v}]

Proof.

Let
\Delta=\{(e,e)\in\mathsf{Exp}\}
be the diagonal relation. We define a relation
{R}\subseteq{\mathsf{Exp}\times\mathsf{Exp}}
, given by the following:

\displaystyle R=\Delta\cup\{

\displaystyle((e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}])[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],e[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}])/\vec{v}])

\displaystyle\mid e,f_{1},\dots,f_{m},g_{1},\dots,g_{n}\in\mathsf{Exp},\vec{v}=(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}}),\vec{w}=(v_{j_{1}},\dots,v_{j_{n}}),

\displaystyle\mathsf{fv}(e)\subseteq\vec{v},\mathsf{fv}(\vec{f})\subseteq\vec{w}\}

We claim that
R
is a bisimulation. For pairs
(e,e)\in\Delta
, the conditions of bisimulation are immediately satisfied.

For the remaining pairs, assume that
(e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}])[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]\rhd u
. In such a case at least one of the following is true:

•

e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}]\rhd u

•

e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}]\rhd w_{j}
for
w_{j}\in\vec{w}
and
g_{j}\rhd u

Since all free variables of
e
are contained in
\vec{v}
and all free variables of
\vec{f}
are contained in
\vec{w}
, we have that all free variables of
e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}]
are also contained in
\vec{w}
, which makes the first case impossible. Through a similar line of reasoning, we can deduce that
e\rhd v_{i}
for some
v_{i}\in\vec{v}
and
f_{i}\rhd w_{j}
. Since
g_{j}\rhd u
, we have that
f_{i}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]\rhd u
. Finally, we have that
e[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{n}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]),\vec{v}]\rhd u
.

Assume that
(e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}])[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h
. Then, at least one of the following is true:

•

e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}]\rhd w_{j}
and
g_{j}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h
.

•

h=h^{\prime}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]
, such that
e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime}

In the first case, through a similar line of reasoning as before, we can conclude that
e\rhd{v_{i}}
for some
v_{i}\in\vec{v}
and
f_{i}\rhd w_{j}
. Hence,
f_{i}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h
. Finally, we can deduce that
e[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}])/\vec{v}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h
. Obviously,
(h,h)\in R
.

In the second case, we have that
e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime}
. There are two subcases, that need to be considered

•

e\rhd v_{i}
and
f_{i}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime}

•

h^{\prime}=h^{\prime\prime}[\vec{f}/\vec{w}]
and
e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime\prime}

In the first subcase, we have that
f_{i}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]
and hence

e[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}])/\vec{v}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]

or equivalently
e[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}])/\vec{v}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h
. As before, of course
(h,h)\in R
.

Finally, moving on to the second subcase, we have that
e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime\prime}
and hence

e[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}])/\vec{v}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h^{\prime\prime}[(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{w}])/\vec{v}]

Recall that
(e[\vec{f}/\vec{v}])[\vec{g}/\vec{w}]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}h
and
h=(h^{\prime\prime}[\vec{f}/\vec{v}])[\vec{g}/\vec{v}]
. Both of those reachable expressions are actually in the relation
R
. The remaining conditions of bisimulation, can be shown via a symmetric argument.
∎

Remark 42

(
[
7
, Example 5.31]
)
.

Let
(X,d)
be a pseudometric space and let
A,B\in P_{\text{fin}}(X)
. Let
\Gamma(A,B)
denote the set of relational couplings of
A
and
B
, namely elements
R\in P_{\text{fin}}(A\times B)
, such that
\pi_{1}(R)=A
and
\pi_{2}(R)=B
. The Hausdorff distance between
A
and
B
can be alternatively presented as:

\mathcal{H}(d)(A,B)=\inf\left\{\sup_{(x,y)\in R}d(x,y)\mid R\in\Gamma(A,B)\right\}

We will make use of the fact that the set of pseudometrics can be equipped with a norm. We write
\overline{\mathbb{R}}=[-\infty,\infty]
for the set of extend reals. For any set
X
, the set of functions
\overline{\mathbb{R}}^{X\times X}
, which is the superset of
D_{X}
, can be seen as a Banach space by means of the sup norm
\|d\|=\sup_{x,y\in X}|d(x,y)|
.

Lemma 43

(
[
52
]
)
.

Hausdorff lifting
\mathcal{H}\colon D_{X}\to D_{P_{\text{fin}}(X)}
is nonexpansive with respect to the metric induced by the sup norm. Namely,

\|\mathcal{H}(d)-\mathcal{H}(d^{\prime})\|\leq\|d-d^{\prime}\|

Lemma 44
.

(-)^{\uparrow}\colon D_{X}\to D_{\Sigma\times X+V}
, the lifitng for
\Sigma\times(-)+V
is contractive with respect to the metric induced by the sup norm. Namely,

\|d^{\uparrow}-d^{\prime\uparrow}\|\leq\frac{1}{2}\|d-d^{\prime}\|

Proof.

For the sake of simplicity, assume that
d^{\prime}\sqsubseteq d
, and hence
d^{\prime\uparrow}\sqsubseteq d^{\uparrow}
. It suffices that we show that for all
u,w\in\Sigma\times X+V
, we have that
d^{\uparrow}(u,w)-d^{\prime\uparrow}(u,w)\leq\frac{1}{2}\|d-d^{\prime}\|
. Recall that in all cases, except when
u=(a,x)
and
w=(a,y)
for some
a\in\Sigma
and
x,y\in X
,
d^{\uparrow}(u,w)=d^{\prime\uparrow}(u,w)
and hence
d^{\uparrow}(u,w)-d^{\prime\uparrow}(u,w)=0\leq\frac{1}{2}\|d-d^{\prime}\|
. In the remaining case, we have that

\displaystyle d^{\uparrow}((a,x),(a,y))-d^{\prime\uparrow}((a,x),(a,y))

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}d(x,y)-\frac{1}{2}d^{\prime}(x,y)

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\|d^{\prime}-d\|

which completes the proof.
∎

Lemma 45
.

\Phi_{\beta}\colon D_{X}\to D_{X}
is contractive with respect to the metric induced by the sup norm, namely

\|\Phi_{\beta}(d)-\Phi_{\beta}(d^{\prime})\|\leq\frac{1}{2}\|d-d^{\prime}\|

Proof.

For the sake of simplicity, assume that
d^{\prime}\sqsubseteq d
and hence
\Phi_{\beta}(d^{\prime})\sqsubseteq\Phi_{\beta}(d)
. It suffices to show that for all
x,y\in X
, we have that
\mathcal{H}(d^{\uparrow})(\beta(x),\beta(y))-\mathcal{H}(d^{\prime\uparrow})(\beta(x),\beta(y))\leq\frac{1}{2}\|d-d^{\prime}\|
. We can combine the previous results and for arbitrary
x,y\in X
obtain the following

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}(d^{\uparrow})(\beta(x),\beta(y))-\mathcal{H}(d^{\prime\uparrow})(\beta(x),\beta(y))

\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{H}(d^{\uparrow})-\mathcal{H}(d^{\prime\uparrow})\|

\displaystyle\leq\|d^{\uparrow}-d^{\prime\uparrow}\|

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\|d-d^{\prime}\|

∎

As a consequence, we have the following

Corollary 46
.

\Phi_{\beta}
has a unique fixpoint.

We will argue that for (locally) finite precharts we can give a simpler characterisation of the behavioural distance relying on Kleene’s theorem for the greatest fixpoint.
Recall that
\omega
-cochain is a sequence
\{d_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}
, such that for all
i\in\mathbb{N}
, we have that
d_{i}\sqsupseteq d_{i+1}
.

Theorem 47

(Kleene fixpoint theorem)
.

Let
(L,\sqsubseteq)
be a partial order where every
\omega
-cochain has an infimum and let
f\colon L\to L
be an endomap that is cocontinuous, namely for all
\omega
-cochains
\{l_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}
, we have that
f\left(\inf_{i\in\mathbb{N}}l_{i}\right)=\inf_{i\in\mathbb{N}}f(l_{i})
. The greatest fixpoint of
f
can be characterised as

\mathsf{gfp}(f)=\inf_{i\in\mathbb{N}}f^{(i)}

where
f^{(0)}=\top
and
f^{(n+1)}=f^{(n)}(f)

Lemma 48
.

For a finite prechart
(X,\beta)
,
\Phi_{\beta}
is cocontinuous.

Proof.

Identical proof to
[
42
, Lemma 20]
.
∎

We can combine the above results into the following statement.
See
27

Proof.

Since
\Phi_{\beta}
has a unique fixpoint, we can rely on a Kleene fixpoint theorem for the greatest fixpoint (
\Cref
thm:kleene), which is preconditioned on
\Phi_{\beta}
being cocontinuous, which is true for finite precharts (
\Cref
lem:cocontinuous). The final formula is given by the fact that in the lattice of pseudometrics, the infima of
\omega
-cochains can be calculated pointwise
[
42
, Lemma 6]
.
∎

Moreover, this can be extended beyond finite charts to the locally finite ones.

Corollary 49
.

For any locally finite prechart
(X,\beta)
, the distance between
x,y\in X
, can be calculated by:

\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=\inf_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\left(\Phi_{\beta}^{(i)}(x,y)\right)

Proof.

Let
\beta^{\prime}
denote
\beta
restricted to
\langle x,y\rangle_{\beta}
.
Since
(X,\beta)
is locally finite, then its subprechart
(\langle x,y\rangle_{\beta},\beta^{\prime})
is finite. Since homomorphisms are isometries, calculating distance between
x
and
y
in
(X,\beta)
is the same as calculating it in
(\langle x,y\rangle_{\beta},\beta)
. Because of
\Cref
lem:cocontinuous,
\Phi_{\beta}
is cocontinuous (when restricted to
\langle x,y\rangle_{\beta^{\prime}}
) and hence we can employ
\Cref
thm:kleene. Since the infima in the lattice of pseudometrics can be calculated pointwise
[
42
, Lemma 6]
, we have that

\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=\mathsf{bd}_{\beta^{\prime}}(x,y)=\inf_{i\in I}\left(\Phi^{(i)}_{\beta^{\prime}}(x,y)\right)

Since
\beta^{\prime}
is a restriction of
\beta
to
{\langle x,y\rangle_{\beta}}
and each
\Phi^{(i)}_{\beta^{\prime}}
makes only use of the states in
\langle x,y\rangle_{\beta}
, we can rewrite the above as
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=\inf_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\left(\Phi_{\beta}^{(i)}(x,y)\right)
as desired.
∎

Lemma 50
.

Let
(X,\beta)
be a locally finite prechart. For all
x,y\in X
,
i\in\mathbb{N}
, either
\Phi_{\beta}^{(i)}=0
or there exists
k\in\mathbb{N}
, such that
\Phi_{\beta}^{(i)}(x,y)=2^{-k}

Proof.

Let
x,y\in X
. We proceed by induction on
i
.

•

If
i=0
, then
\Phi^{(0)}_{\beta}(x,y)=1=2^{0}
, if
x\not=0
or
\Phi^{(0)}_{\beta}(x,y)=0
, otherwise.

•

If
i=j+1
, then unrolling the definition of
\Phi_{\beta}^{(j+1)}
yields the following:

\Phi^{j+1}_{\beta}(x,y)=\max\left\{\sup_{u\in\beta(x)}\inf_{w\in\beta(y)}{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}^{\uparrow}(u,w),\sup_{w\in\beta(y)}\inf_{u\in\beta(x)}{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}^{\uparrow}(w,u)\right\}

For any two transitions
u=(a,x^{\prime})
and
w=(a,y^{\prime})
with the same prefix, the following holds:

{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}^{\uparrow}(u,w)=\frac{1}{2}{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})

We can apply the induction hypothesis, which states that one of the following is true:

–

{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=0
, which entails that
{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}^{\uparrow}(u,w)=0
.

–

There exists a
k\in N
, such that
{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=2^{-k}
. This implies that
{\Phi^{(j)}_{\beta}}^{\uparrow}(u,w)=2^{-(k+1)}
.

Since the infima range over finite sets, their values are either
1=2^{0}
if the sets are empty or are one of the values from the set, which we have shown to be of the desired form. Similarly, suprema range over finite sets and are either
0
for empty sets or are on of the values from the set, which are in the desired form. Taking the maximum of values in the desired form, still results in a value in the desired form.∎

Lemma 51
.

Let
(X,\beta)
be a locally finite prechart and let
x,y\in X
, such that
\neg(x\sim y)
. There exists
i\in\mathbb{N}
, such that
\Phi_{\beta}^{(i)}(x,y)=\Phi^{(i+1)}_{\beta}(x,y)

Proof.

Assume that for all
i\in\mathbb{N}
,
\Phi_{\beta}^{(i)}(x,y)\neq\Phi^{(i+1)}_{\beta}(x,y)
. Essentially, that means we have an infinite, strictly decreasing
\omega
-cochain
\{\Phi^{(i)}_{\beta}(x,y)\}_{i\in I}
. By
\Cref
lem:distance_power_of_two, we know that the values of the chain are either
0
or
2^{-k}
. Since all the values of the chain are nonegative, if any of it is equal to zero
0
, we reach a contradiction, as the chain would have to contain values strictly below
0
. Hence, we can safely assume that the chain is in the form
\{1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4},\dots\}
. But in such a case its infimum is
0
, contradicting the assumption.
∎

Corollary 52
.

Let
(X,\beta)
be a locally finite prechart and let
x,y\in X
. If
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)>0
, then there exists an
i\in\mathbb{N}
, such that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=\Phi^{(i)}_{\beta}(x,y)

Proof.

If
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)>0
, we have that
\neg(x\sim y)
and using
\Cref
lem:chain_stabilises, we know that the chain of approximants stabilises and hence the infimum of the chain is equal to the point where it stabilises.
∎

Lemma 53
.

Let
(X,\beta)
be a prechart. For any
x,y\in X
, we have that

x\sim^{(k)}y\iff\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)\leq 2^{-k}

Proof.

By induction on
k
. The base case is trivial, as we immediately have that
x\sim^{(0)}y
and
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)\leq 2^{0}=1
.

For the inductive step assume that for some
k^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}
, the induction hypothesis holds. First, assume that
x\sim^{(k^{\prime}+1)}y
. Unrolling the definition of stratification of bisimilarity, we have that

•

If
x\rhd v
, then
y\rhd v

•

If
x\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}x^{\prime}
, then there exists
y^{\prime}
such that
y\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}y^{\prime}
and
x\sim^{(k^{\prime})}y
.

and symmetrically.

We want to show that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}
. We can unroll the definition of
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}
and rewrite the desired result as

\sup_{u\in\beta(x)}\left(\inf_{w\in\beta(y)}\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(u,w)\right)\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}\quad\wedge\quad\sup_{w\in\beta(y)}\left(\inf_{u\in\beta(x)}\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(w,u)\right)\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}

We focus on the left hand side of the conjunction above, as the right hand side is symmetric. We are aiming to show that

\forall{u\in\beta(x)}\ldotp~\inf_{w\in\beta(y)}\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(u,w)\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}

Let
u\in V
. By the assumption, we know that also
u\in B(y)
, which means that

\inf_{w\in\beta(y)}\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(u,w)=0\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}

Now, let
u\in\Sigma\times X
, i.e.
u=(a,x^{\prime})
. By the assumption, we know that there exists
y^{\prime}\in X
, such that
(a,y^{\prime})\in\beta(y)
and
x^{\prime}\sim^{(k^{\prime})}y^{\prime}
. By induction hypothesis, we know that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\leq 2^{-k^{\prime}}
. Hence, we have that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}((a,x^{\prime}),(a,x^{\prime}))\leq\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2^{-k^{\prime}}=2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}
. Hence, we again have that

\forall{u\in\beta(x)}\ldotp~\inf_{w\in\beta(y)}\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(u,w)\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}

Now, for the converse assume that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}
. Through a similar line of reasoning, as before, we have that

\forall{u\in\beta(x)}\ldotp~\inf_{w\in\beta(y)}\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(u,w)\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}

Assume that
x\rhd v
, i.e.
v\in\beta(x)
. Assume that
\neg(y\rhd v)
. That means that for all
w\in\beta(y)
, we have that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(v,w)=1
and hence
\inf_{w\in\beta(y)}\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}(v,w)=1
, which contradicts the assumption as
1>2^{-{(k^{\prime}+1)}}
. Hence,
y\rhd v
.

Now, assume that
x\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}x^{\prime}
, i.e.
(a,x^{\prime})\in\beta(y)
. Through a similar argument as before, we know that there must exist
(a,y^{\prime})\in\beta(y)
, such that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}((a,x^{\prime}),(a,y^{\prime}))\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}
. Unrolling the definitions of
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}^{\uparrow}
, we obtain
\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\leq 2^{-(k^{\prime}+1)}
and hence
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\leq 2^{-k^{\prime}}
. Using the induction hypothesis, we get that
x^{\prime}\sim^{(k^{\prime})}y^{\prime}
as desired. The remaining part of the proof is symmetric and hence is omitted.
∎

Theorem 54
.

Let
(X,\beta)
be a locally finite prechart and let
x,y\in X
. The behavioural distance between
x
and
y
is given by:

\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=\begin{cases}0&\text{ if }x\sim y\\
2^{-n}&\text{ if }n\text{ is the largest number such that }x\sim^{(n)}y\end{cases}

Proof.

For the first case, because of
\Cref
thm:beh_dist, if
x\sim y
, then
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=0
. For the converse, if
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=0
, we have that
x\sim^{(k)}y
for all
k\in\mathbb{N}
and hence by
[
24
, Theorem 2.1]
, it holds that
x\sim y
.

In the second case, because of
\Cref
lem:chain_stabilises, we know that if
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)>0
, then the behavioural distance is equal to some element of the chain of approximants. By
\Cref
lem:distance_power_of_two, we know that all non-zero elements of that chain are equal to
2^{-k}
, for some
k\in\mathbb{N}
. Combining it with
\Cref
lem:bound_on_stratified_bisim yields the desired result.
For the converse, if
n\in N
is the largest number such that
x\sim^{(n)}y
, then because of
\Cref
lem:bound_on_stratified_bisim, we have that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)\leq 2^{-n}
. Assume that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)=0
. In such a case, using
\Cref
lem:bound_on_stratified_bisim, we could conclude that
x\sim^{(n+1)}y
, which would lead to contradiction. Hence,
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)>0
. Because of
\Cref
lem:chain_stabilises, we have that
\mathsf{bd}_{\beta}(x,y)
is equal to some power of two. Combining that with
\Cref
lem:bound_on_stratified_bisim again yields the desired result.∎

Lemma 55
.

Let
(X,\beta)
,
(Y,\gamma)
and
(Z,\zeta)
be arbitrary precharts, such that there exist homomorphisms
f\colon X\to Z
and
g\colon Y\to Z
.
For all
p\in\mathbb{N}
,
(x,y)\in X\times Y
, we have that if
x\sim^{(p)}y
then
f(x)\sim^{(p)}g(y)
.

Proof.

Recall that if
f\colon X\to Y
is a homomorphism, then
G(f)=\{(x,f(x))\mid x\in X\}
is a bisimulation, which implies that for all
p\in\mathbb{N}
,
x\in X
we have that
x\sim^{(p)}f(x)

[
24
, Theorem 2.1]
. Similarly, for all
p\in\mathbb{N}
,
y\in Y
, we have that
y\sim^{(p)}g(y)
. Since relations constituting the stratification of bisimilarity are all equivalence relations
[
24
]
, we know that if
x\sim^{(p)}y
,
x\sim^{(p)}f(x)
and
y\sim^{(p)}g(y)
jointly imply that
f(x)\sim^{(p)}g(y)
for all
p\in\mathbb{N}
and
(x,y)\in X\times Y
, which completes the proof.
∎

See
8

Proof.

Immediately follows from
\Cref
thm:concrete_distance and
\Cref
lem:hom_stratification.
∎
