Appendix C
Semantics

Lemma 56
.

Let
f\colon m\to n
,
g\colon n\to p
,
h\colon p\to q
. We have that:

1.

(f;g);h=f;(g;h)

2.

\mathrm{id}_{m};f=f

3.

f;\mathrm{id}_{n}=f

Proof.

We respectively prove each of the properties.

1.

\displaystyle(f;g);h

\displaystyle=(f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{v}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{v}]);h

\displaystyle=\left((f_{1}[\vec{g}/\vec{v}])[\vec{h},\vec{v}],\dots,(f_{m}[\vec{g}/\vec{v}])[\vec{h},\vec{v}]\right)

\displaystyle=\left(f_{1}[(g_{1}[\vec{h}/\vec{v}],\dots,g_{n}[\vec{h}/\vec{v}])/\vec{v}],\dots,f_{m}[(g_{1}[\vec{h}/\vec{v}],\dots,g_{n}[\vec{h}/\vec{v}])/\vec{v}]\right)

(
\Cref
lem:subst_lemma)

\displaystyle=\left(f_{1}[\vec{(g;h)}/\vec{v}],\dots f_{m}[\vec{(g;h)}/\vec{v}]\right)

\displaystyle=f;(g;h)

2.

id_{m};f=(v_{1}[\vec{f}/\vec{v}],\dots,v_{m}[\vec{f}/\vec{v}])=(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=f

3.

f;id_{n}=(f_{1}[\vec{v}/\vec{v}],\dots,f_{m}[\vec{v}/\vec{v}]])=(f_{1},\dots,f_{m})=f

∎

Lemma 57
.

\mathsf{RegBeh}
has binary coproducts. In particular, given
k,l\in\mathbb{N}
, the inclusions
\mathsf{inl}_{k,l}\colon k\to k+l
and
\mathsf{inr}_{k,l}\colon l\to k+l
are given by
\mathsf{inl}_{k,l}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{k})
and
\mathsf{inr}_{k,l}=(v_{k+1},\dots,v_{k+l})
respectively, while the mediating map is given by pairing.

Proof.

Let
f\colon k\to m
and
g\colon l\to m
. We can safely assume that
f=(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})
and
g=(g_{1},\dots,g_{l})
. Recall that
\mathsf{inl}_{k,l}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{k})
and
\mathsf{inr}_{k,l}=(v_{k+1},\dots,v_{k+l})
. For the existence proof, define
\langle f,g\rangle\colon k+l\to m
as a
k+l
-tuple
(f_{1},\dots,f_{k},g_{1},\dots,g_{l})
. We show that that the coproduct diagram commutes. We start from the left triangular subdiagram.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{k+l}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{inl}_{k+l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{inr}_{k+l}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle f,g\rangle}

\displaystyle\mathsf{inl}_{k,l};\langle f,g\rangle

\displaystyle=(v_{1},\dots,v_{k});(f_{1},\dots f_{k},g_{1},\dots,g_{l})

\displaystyle=(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})

\displaystyle=f

Similarly, for the right subdiagram, we have that:

\displaystyle\mathsf{inr}_{k,l};\langle f,g\rangle

\displaystyle=(v_{k+1},\dots,v_{k+l});(f_{1},\dots f_{k},g_{1},\dots,g_{l})

\displaystyle=(g_{1},\dots,g_{l})

\displaystyle=g

For the uniqueness proof, assume that there exists a map
h\colon k+l\to m
, which makes the coproduct diagram commute. We can safely assume that
h=(h_{1},\dots,h_{k+l})
.
Since
\mathsf{inl}_{k,l};h=f
and
\mathsf{inr}_{k,l};h=g
, we have that:

\displaystyle(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})

\displaystyle=f

\displaystyle=\mathsf{inl}_{k,l};h

\displaystyle=(v_{1},\dots,v_{k});(h_{1},\dots,h_{k+l})

\displaystyle=(h_{1},\dots,h_{k})

Similarly, we have that:

\displaystyle(g_{1},\dots,g_{l})

\displaystyle=f

\displaystyle=\mathsf{inr}_{k,l};h

\displaystyle=(v_{k+1},\dots,v);(h_{1},\dots,h_{k+l})

\displaystyle=(h_{k+1},\dots,h_{k+l})

Hence,
h=(f_{1},\dots,f_{k},g_{1},\dots,g_{l})=\langle f,g\rangle
as desired.
∎

Lemma 58
.

0
is the initial object of
\mathsf{RegBeh}
.

Proof.

For any
n\in\mathbb{N}
, the unique universal arrow is given by
0_{n}
, which immediately completes the proof.
∎

Given
f\colon k\to l
and
g\colon m\to n
, we can define their
separated sum

f\oplus g\colon k+m\to l+n
given by the unique mediating arrow in the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{k+m}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces m}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces l}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{l+n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{inl}_{k,m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\oplus g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{inr}_{k,m}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{inl}_{l,n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{inr}_{l,n}}

We can define
f\oplus g
concretely by setting
f\oplus g=\langle f,g[(v_{l+1},\dots,v_{l+n})/(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})]\rangle
.

Proposition 59
.

(\mathsf{RegBeh},\oplus,0)
is a strict monoidal category.

Proof.

We verify that associators and unitors are strict equalities. Let
f\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(k,l),g\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,n),h\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(o,p)
. For the left unitor, we have the following:

\displaystyle 0\oplus f

\displaystyle=()\oplus(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})

(def. of
0
and
\oplus
)

\displaystyle=(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})=f

Similarly, for the right unitor, we have that:

\displaystyle f\oplus 0

\displaystyle=()\oplus(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})

(def. of
0
and
\oplus
)

\displaystyle=(f_{1},\dots,f_{k})=f

Finally, for the associator we have that:

\displaystyle(f\oplus g)\oplus h

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(f_{1},\dots,f_{k},g_{1}[(v_{l+1},\dots,v_{l+n})/\vec{v}],\dots,g_{m}[(v_{l+1},\dots,v_{l+n})/\vec{v}])\oplus h

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(f_{1},\dots,f_{k},g_{1}[(v_{l+1},\dots,v_{l+n})/\vec{v}],\dots,g_{m}[(v_{l+1},\dots,v_{l+n})/\vec{v}],

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad h_{1}[(v_{l+n+1},\dots,v_{l+n+p})/\vec{v}],\dots,h_{o}[(v_{l+n+1},\dots,v_{l+n+p})/\vec{v}])

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle f\oplus(g_{1}[(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})/\vec{v}],\dots,g_{m}[(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})/\vec{v}],

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad h_{1}[(v_{n+1},\dots,v_{n+p})/\vec{v}],\dots,h_{o}[(v_{n+1},\dots,v_{n+p})/\vec{v}])

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle f\oplus(g_{1},\dots,g_{m},

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad h_{1}[(v_{n+1},\dots,v_{n+p})/\vec{v}],\dots,h_{o}[(v_{n+1},\dots,v_{n+p})/\vec{v}])

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle f\oplus(g\oplus h)

The intermediate steps in the calculation above follow from the definition of
\oplus
.
∎

C.1
Conway Theories

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a category with finite coproducts, whose objects are natural numbers. We call
\mathcal{C}
a
preiteration theory
if for every morphism
f\colon n\to p+n
, there exists a morphism
f^{\dagger}_{n,p}\colon n\to p
called
dagger
. We will often omit the subscripts and write
f^{\dagger}
, when
n
and
m
are clear from the context. Note that the definition does not impose any conditions on the dagger. However,
f\colon 0\to p
, when always we have that
f_{0,p}^{\dagger}=0_{p}
.

Definition 60

(
[
17
, Definition 3.1]
)
.

A Conway Theory is a preiteration theory, in which the following conditions are satisfied

•

(Scalar parameter identity)

(f;(g\oplus\mathrm{id}_{1}))^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger};g

for all
f\colon 1\to p+1
,
g\colon p\to q

•

(Scalar composition identity)

(f;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},g\rangle)^{\dagger}=f;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},(g;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},f\rangle)^{\dagger}\rangle

for all
f,g\colon 1\to p+1

•

(Scalar double dagger identity)

f^{\dagger\dagger}=(f;(\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus\nabla_{1}))^{\dagger}

for all
f\colon 1\to p+2

•

(Scalar pairing identity)

\langle f,g\rangle^{\dagger}=\langle f^{\dagger};\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},h^{\dagger}\rangle,h^{\dagger}\rangle

for all
f\colon n\to p+1+n
,
g\colon 1\to p+1+n
where

h=g;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p+1},f^{\dagger}\rangle\colon 1\to p+1

Remark 61

(
[
17
, Remark 3.2]
)
.

Note that in order to define a Conway theory it suffices to define
f^{\dagger}\colon 1\to p
for all
f\colon 1\to p+1
that satisfies first three axioms of
\Cref
def:conway_theory and use
scalar pairing identity
to inductively define
(-)^{\dagger}
.

Because of the above, we can define a dagger on
\mathsf{RegBeh}
through the following:

Definition 62
.

Given
f\colon 1\to p+1
in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
, we define

f^{\dagger}=\mu v_{p+1}.f

Lemma 63

(
[
46
, Theorem 2]
)
.

Terms of Milner’s Algebra of Regular Behaviours (modulo bisimilarity) satisfy the following rules:

1.

\mu v_{z}.\left(e[(v_{z},v_{z})/(v_{j},v_{k})]\right)=\mu v_{j}.\mu v_{k}.e
for any
v_{z}
not free in
e

2.

\mu v_{j}.\left(e[f/v_{j}]\right)=e[\mu v_{x}.\left(f[e/v_{j}]\right)/v_{j}]

Corollary 64
.

The dagger on
\mathsf{RegBeg}
satisfies
scalar composition
and
scalar double dagger
identities.

Proof.

Follows from
\Cref
lem:recursion-substitution.
∎

Lemma 65
.

Let
f\colon 1\to 1+p
,
g\colon p\to g
be morphisms in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
. Then,

(f;(g\oplus\mathrm{id}_{1}))^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger};g

Proof.

\displaystyle(f;(g\oplus\mathrm{id}_{1}))^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=(f[(g_{1},\dots,g_{p},v_{q+1})/(v_{1},\dots,v_{p},v_{p+1})])^{\dagger}

(Def. of
\oplus
)

\displaystyle=\mu v_{q+1}.\big(f[(g_{1},\dots,g_{p},v_{q+1})/(v_{1},\dots,v_{p},v_{p+1})]\big)

(Def. of
\dagger
)

\displaystyle=\mu v_{q+1}.\big(f[v_{q+1}/v_{p+1}][\vec{g}/\vec{v}]\big)

(
[
35
, Lemma 5.6 2.]
)

\displaystyle=(\mu v_{q+1}.f[v_{q+1}/v_{p+1}])[\vec{g}/\vec{v}]

(
\Cref
def:subset)

\displaystyle=(\mu v_{p+1}.f)[\vec{g}/\vec{v}]

(
[
35
, Proposition 4.6 5.]
)

\displaystyle=f^{\dagger}[\vec{g}/\vec{v}]

(Def. of
\dagger
)

\displaystyle=f^{\dagger};g

∎

Lemma 66
.

Let
f,g\colon 1\to 1+p
be morphisms of
\mathsf{RegBeh}
. Then,

(f;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},g\rangle)^{\dagger}=f;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},(g;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},f\rangle)^{\dagger}\rangle

Proof.

\displaystyle(f;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},g\rangle)^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=\big(f[(v_{1},\dots,v_{p},g)/\vec{v}]\big)^{\dagger}

\displaystyle=\mu v_{p+1}.\big(f[(v_{1},\dots,v_{p},g)/\vec{v}]\big)

\displaystyle=\mu v_{p+1}.\big(f[g/v_{p+1}]\big)

\displaystyle=f[\mu v_{p+1}.\left(g[f/v_{p+1}]\right)/v_{p+1}]

(
\Cref
lem:recursion-substitution 2.)

\displaystyle=f[\mu v_{p+1}.\left(g[(v_{1},\dots,v_{n},f)/(v_{1},\dots,v_{n},v_{p+1})]\right)/v_{p+1}]

\displaystyle=f[\mu v_{p+1}.(g;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},f\rangle)/v_{p+1}]

\displaystyle=f[(g;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},f\rangle)^{\dagger}/v_{p+1}]

\displaystyle=f;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},(g;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus 0_{1},f\rangle)^{\dagger}\rangle\qed

And the
scalar double dagger identity
.

Lemma 67
.

Let
f\colon 1\to 2+p
be a morphism of
\mathsf{RegBeh}
. Then,

f^{\dagger\dagger}=(f;(\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus\nabla_{1}))^{\dagger}

Proof.

\displaystyle f^{\dagger\dagger}

\displaystyle=\mu v_{p+1}.(\mu v_{p+2}.f)

\displaystyle=\mu v_{p+1}.\left(f[(v_{p+1},v_{p+1})/(v_{p+1},v_{p+2})]\right)

(
\Cref
lem:recursion-substitution 1.)

\displaystyle=\mu v_{p+1}.\left(f;(\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus\nabla_{1})\right)

\displaystyle=(f;(\mathrm{id}_{p}\oplus\nabla_{1}))^{\dagger}

∎

Lemma 68
.

\mathsf{RegBeh}
is a Conway Theory.

Proof.

Follows from
\Cref
conway1,
\Cref
conway2 and
\Cref
conway3.
∎

C.2
Trace-fixpoint correspondence

Turns out, that having a category
\mathcal{C}
with finite coproducts and equipped with a dagger operator satisfying the axioms of Conway Theories is synonymous with
\mathcal{C}
being traced symmetr ic monoidal category. This is captured by the following theorem that was independently proved by Hasegawa
[
23
]
and Haghverdi
[
22
]
. The formulation of Hasegawa is phrased dually via the setting of products and cartesian categories.

Theorem 69

(
[
22
, Proposition 3.1.9]
)
.

For any category with finite coproducts, to give a Conway operator is to give a trace (where finite coproducts are taken as the monoidal structure).

That bijective correspondence is concretely given by the following:

\displaystyle\frac{f\colon n\to p+n}{f^{\dagger}=\mathsf{Tr}^{n}_{n,p}(\nabla_{n};f)\colon n\to p}\qquad\frac{g\colon p+n\to q+n}{\mathsf{Tr}^{n}_{p,q}(g)=\mathsf{inl}_{p,n};(g;\langle\mathrm{id}_{q},\mathsf{inr}_{q+p,n}\rangle)^{\dagger}\colon p\to q}

C.3
Int construction

Given a traced symmetric monoidal category
\mathcal{C}
, we can construct a compact closed category
\mathbf{Int}(\mathcal{C})
. The objects of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathcal{C})
are the pairs
(A^{+},A^{-})
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
. Morphisms
f
from
(A^{+},A^{-})
to
(B^{+},B^{-})
are the morphisms
f\colon A^{+}\otimes B^{-}\to A^{-}\otimes B^{+}
of
\mathcal{C}
. The identity of any object
(A^{+},A^{-})
is given by the symmetry of
\mathcal{C}
, namely
\mathrm{id}_{(A^{+},A^{-})}=\sigma_{A^{+},A^{-}}
. The composition
f;g\colon(A^{+},A^{-})\to(C^{+},C^{-})
of morphisms
f\colon(A^{+},A^{-})\to(B^{+},B^{-})
and
g\colon(B^{+},B^{-})\to(C^{+},C^{-})
is defined as

\mathsf{Tr}^{B^{-}\otimes B^{+}}_{A^{+}\otimes C^{-},A^{-}\otimes C^{+}}(\alpha;(f\otimes g);\beta)

in
\mathcal{C}
, where
\alpha=(\mathrm{id}_{A^{+}}\otimes\sigma_{C^{-},B^{-}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B^{+}});(\mathrm{id}_{A^{+}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B^{-}}\otimes\sigma_{C^{-},B^{+}})
and
\beta=(\mathrm{id}_{A^{-}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B^{+}}\otimes\sigma_{B^{-},C^{+}});(\mathrm{id}_{A^{-}}\otimes\sigma_{B^{+},C^{+}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B^{-}});(\mathrm{id}_{A^{-}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{C^{+}}\otimes\sigma_{B^{+},B^{-}})
.

\mathbf{Int}(\mathcal{C})
is equipped with the monoidal structure. The tensor product of
(A^{+},A^{-})
and
(B^{+},B^{-})
is given by taking the tensor product of
\mathcal{C}
pointwise, namely
(A^{+}\otimes B^{+},A^{-}\otimes B^{-})
. The unit of that monoidal product is given by
(I,I)
, where
I
is the unit of the monoidal product on
\mathcal{C}
. The tensor product
f\otimes g\colon(A^{+}\otimes C^{+},B^{-}\otimes D^{-})\to(A^{-}\otimes C^{-},B^{+}\otimes D^{+})
of
f\colon(A^{+},A^{-})\to(B^{+},B^{-})
and
g\colon(C^{+},C^{-})\to(C^{+},C^{-})\to(D^{+},D^{-})
is given by:

f\otimes g=(\mathrm{id}_{A^{+}}\otimes\sigma_{C^{+},B^{-}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{D^{-}});(f\otimes g);(\mathrm{id}_{A^{-}}\otimes\sigma_{B^{+},C^{-}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{D^{+}})

The dual
(A^{+},A^{-})^{\ast}
of
(A^{+},A^{-})
is given by exchanging the components, that is by
(A^{-},A^{+})
. Then, the unit
\eta_{(A^{+},A^{-})}\colon(I,I)\to(A^{+},A^{-})\otimes(A^{+},A^{-})^{\ast}
is a morphism
\sigma_{A^{-},A^{+}}\colon A^{-}\otimes A^{+}\to A^{+}\otimes A^{-}
. The counit
\epsilon_{(A^{+},A^{-})}\colon(A^{+},A^{-})^{\ast}\otimes(A^{+},A^{-})\to(I,I)
can be similarly given by
\sigma_{A^{-},A^{+}}\colon A^{-}\otimes A^{+}\to A^{+}\otimes A^{-}
in
\mathcal{C}
.

\mathbf{Int}(\mathcal{C})
is equipped with a canonical trace, which takes a morphism
f\colon(A^{+},A^{-})\otimes(U^{+},U-)\to(B^{+},B^{-})\otimes(U^{+},U-)
to

\mathsf{Tr}^{(U^{+},U^{-})}_{(A^{+},A^{-}),(B^{+},B^{-})}(f)=\left(\mathrm{id}_{(A^{+},A-)}\otimes\eta_{(U^{+},U-)}\right);\left(f\otimes\mathrm{id}_{{(U^{+},U^{-})}^{\ast}}\right);\left(\mathrm{id}_{(B^{+},B^{-})}\otimes\epsilon_{(U^{+},U-)}\right)

C.4
Pseudometric structure on the semantic category

Lemma 70
.

Let
i_{1},\dots,i_{m}\in\mathbb{N}
. For all
n\in\mathbb{N}
and for all
e,f,g_{1},\dots,g_{m},h_{1},\dots,h_{m}\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
, we have that

e\sim^{(n)}f\wedge\bigwedge_{j=1}^{j\leq m}g_{j}\sim^{(n)}h_{j}\implies e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\sim^{(n)}f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]

Proof.

Base case holds immediately, since we always have that
e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\sim^{(0)}f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]
for all
e,f,g_{1},\dots,g_{j},h_{1},\dots,h_{j}\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}

Assume that
e\sim^{(n+1)}f
,
g_{j}\sim^{(n+1)}h_{j}
for all
j\in\{1,\dots,m\}
. For the successor case assume that
e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\sim^{(n)}f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]
. We will argue that

e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\sim^{(n+1)}f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]

To do so, we will study the operational semantics of both (equivalence classes of) expressions.

Assume that
e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\rhd v_{k}
. Using
\Cref
rem:semantic-substitution, we can observe that it is the case if any of the following is true:

•

e\rhd v_{k}
and
v_{k}\notin\{v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{j}}\}

•

e\rhd v_{i_{l}}
for some
v_{i_{l}}\in\{v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{j}}\}
and
g_{l}\rhd{v_{k}}

Consider the first subcase. Since
e\rhd v_{k}
(for some
k\notin\{v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{j}}\}
) and by assumption
e\sim^{n+1}f
, we have that
f\rhd{v_{k}}
and hence
f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{j})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{j}})]\rhd v_{k}
. Now, consider the second subcase. By a similar line of reasoning, we can obtain
f\rhd v_{l}
and
h_{l}\rhd v_{k}
. Hence, again we have that
f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{j})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{j}})]\rhd v_{k}
. In other words, we have shown that
e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\rhd v_{k}
implies
f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{j})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{j}})]\rhd v_{k}
. One can easily obtain a reverse implication through a symmetric proof.

Now, assume that
e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}s
. Using
\Cref
rem:semantic-substitution, we know that such transition can be made only if any of the following is true:

•

s=e^{\prime}[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]
, for some
e^{\prime}
such that
e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}e^{\prime}

•

For some
v_{i_{l}}
, such that
v_{i_{l}}\in\{v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}}\}
, we have that
e\rhd v_{l}
and
g_{l}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}s

Consider the first subcase. We know that
f\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}f^{\prime}
and
e^{\prime}\sim^{(n)}f^{\prime}
. Using the induction hypothesis, we can conclude that

e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}})]\sim^{(n)}f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}})]

Hence, there exists a
t
, such that
f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}})]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}t
, such that
s\sim^{(n)}t
.

Now, consider the second subcase. We can easily conclude that
f\rhd v_{l}
and
h_{l}\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}t
, with
s\sim^{(n)}t
.

In other words, we have show that
e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}})]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}s
, then there exists
t
, such that
f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}})]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}t
, such that
s\sim^{(n)}t
. The reverse implication can be again shown via a symmetric argument. Combining all of the above, we can conclude that

e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}})]\sim^{(n+1)}f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m})/(v_{i_{1}},\dots,v_{i_{m}})]\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}t

∎

Corollary 71
.

Let
e,f,g_{1},\dots,g_{m},h_{1},\dots,g_{m}\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
. Then,

\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}\left(e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m}/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})],f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m}/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\right)\leq\max\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(e,f),\max_{j\in\{1,\dots,m\}}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(g_{j},h_{j})\}\}

Proof.

If the right hand side of the inequality is equal to zero, then we have that
e\sim f
and
g_{j}\sim h_{j}
for
j\in\{1,\dots,m\}
. We can use
\Cref
lem:congruence, to conclude that
e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m}/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]\sim f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m}/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})]
and hence
\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(e[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m}/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})],f[(h_{1},\dots,h_{m}/(v_{i_{1}},\dots v_{i_{m}})])=0
, which implies nonexpansivity.

If the right hand side is greater than zero, we can employ the characterisation of
\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}
from
\Cref
thm:concrete_distance and use
\Cref
lem:subst-stratified-bisim to conclude the desired result.
∎

Lemma 72
.

Let
e,f\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim_{\partial}}
. Then, for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
, we have that

e\sim^{(n)}f\implies\mu v_{x}.e\sim^{(n)}\mu v_{x}.f

Proof.

Base case holds immediately, as
\mu v_{x}.e\sim^{(0)}\mu v_{x}.f
for all
e,f\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
.

Assume that
e\sim^{(n+1)}f
. For the successor case assume that
\mu v_{x}.e\sim^{(n)}\mu v_{x}.f
. We will argue that
\mu v_{x}.e\sim^{(n+1)}\mu v_{x}.f
.

Assume that
\mu v_{x}.e\rhd v_{k}
. It is only the case, when
e\rhd{v_{k}}
and
v_{k}\neq v_{x}
. Since
e\sim^{(n+1)}f
, then
f\rhd{v_{k}}
and hence
\mu v_{x}.f\rhd v_{k}
. In other words,
\mu v_{x}.e\rhd v_{k}
implies
\mu v_{x}.f\rhd v_{k}
. The reverse implication can be easily obtained via a symmetric proof.

Now, assume that
\mu v_{x}.e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}s
. It is the case, when
e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}e^{\prime}
and
s=e^{\prime}[\mu v_{x}.e/v_{x}]
. Since
e\sim^{(n+1)}f
, then there exists
f^{\prime}
, such that
f\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}f^{\prime}
and
e\sim^{(n)}f
. We can now use induction hypothesis and
\Cref
lem:subst-stratified-bisim and conclude that
e^{\prime}[\mu v_{x}.e/v_{x}]\sim^{(n)}f^{\prime}[\mu v.f/v_{x}]
. Moreover, we have that
\mu v.xf\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}f^{\prime}[\mu v_{x}.f/v_{x}]
. Hence, if
\mu v_{x}.e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}s
, then there exists
t
, such that
\mu v_{x}.f\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}t
and
s\sim^{(n)}t
. A reverse implication can be obtained via a symmetric proof.

Combing the above, allows us to conclude that
\mu v_{x}.e\sim^{(n+1)}\mu v_{x}.f
.
∎

Corollary 73
.

Let
e,f\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
. We have that

\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(\mu v_{x}.e,\mu v_{x}.f)\leq\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(e,f)

Proof.

Analogous proof to
\Cref
cor:seq_nexp, but utilising
\Cref
lem:rec_startified_bisim instead.
∎

Lemma 74
.

Let
e,f\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
. Then for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
,
a\in\Sigma
, we have that

e\sim^{(n)}f\implies a.e\sim^{(n+1)}a.f

Proof.

a.e
does not output anything and so does
a.f
. Now, assume that
a.e\mathrel{\!\raisebox{-2.0pt}{
$\xrightarrow{a}$
}\!}e^{\prime}
. Then, the only possibility is that
e^{\prime}=e
. We can match that transition with an expression
a.f
that performs an
a
-labelled transition to
f
. Since
e\sim^{(n)}f
, then
a.e\sim^{(n+1)}a.f
. The remaining condition works through a symmetric line of reasoning.
∎

Corollary 75
.

Let
e,f\in{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
. Then for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
,
a\in\Sigma
, we have that

\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(a.e,a.f)\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(e,f)

Proof.

We employ the characterisation from
\Cref
thm:concrete_distance. If
e\sim f
, then by
\Cref
lem:congruence we are done. Otherwise, we have that
\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(e,f)=2^{-k}
and
e\sim^{(k)}_{\overline{\partial}}f
for some
k\in\mathbb{N}
. By applying
\Cref
cor:prefixing_discounts, we get that
a.e\sim^{(k+1)}a.f
and hence
\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(e,f)\leq 2^{-(k+1)}=\frac{1}{2}2^{-k}=\frac{1}{2}\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(e,f)
, as desired.
∎

Lemma 76
.

Sequential composition in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
is nonexpansive.

Proof.

Let
f,h\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(n,m)
and
g,i\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,k)
.

\displaystyle d^{n,k}(f;g,h;i)

\displaystyle=\sup_{1\leq j\leq n}\left\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}\left(\langle f_{j}[(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})/(v_{1},\dots,v_{m})],h_{j}[(i_{1},\dots,i_{m})/(v_{1},\dots,v_{m})]\right)\right\}

\displaystyle\leq\sup_{1\leq j\leq n}\left\{\max\left\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(f_{j},h_{j}),\sup_{1\leq l\leq m}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(g_{l},i_{l})\}\right\}\right\}

(
\Cref
cor:seq_nexp)

\displaystyle=\max\{\sup_{1\leq j\leq n}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(f_{j},h_{j})\},\sup_{1\leq l\leq m}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(g_{l},i_{l})\}\}

\displaystyle=\max\{d^{n,m}(f,h),d^{m,k}(g,i)\}

∎

Lemma 77
.

Let
f,f^{\prime}\colon m\to k
,
g,g^{\prime}\colon n\to k
be morphisms of
\mathsf{RegBeh}
. We have that
d^{m+n,k}(\langle f,g\rangle,\langle f^{\prime},g^{\prime}\rangle)\leq\max\{d^{m,k}(f,f^{\prime}),d^{n,k}(g,g^{\prime})\}

Proof.

\displaystyle d^{m+n,k}(\langle f,g\rangle,\langle f^{\prime},g^{\prime}\rangle)

\displaystyle=d^{m+n,k}((f_{1},\dots,f_{m},g_{1},\dots,g_{n}),(f^{\prime}_{1},\dots,f^{\prime}_{m},g^{\prime}_{1},\dots,g^{\prime}_{n}))

\displaystyle=\max\left\{d^{m,k}((f_{1},\dots,f_{m}),(f^{\prime}_{1},\dots,f^{\prime}_{m})),d^{n,k}((g_{1},\dots,g_{m}),(g^{\prime}_{1},\dots,g^{\prime}_{m}))\right\}

\displaystyle\leq\max\left\{d^{m,k}(f,f^{\prime}),d^{n,k}(g,g^{\prime})\right\}

∎

Lemma 78
.

The coproduct in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
is nonexpansive.

Proof.

Let
f,h\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(k,m)
and
g,i\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(l,n)
. Given
j\in\mathbb{N}
, such that
1\leq j\leq l
, we define

g^{\prime}_{j}=g_{j}[(v_{m+1},\dots,v_{m+n})/(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})]

Similarly, we write

i^{\prime}_{j}=i_{j}[(v_{m+1},\dots,v_{m+n})/(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})]

Using
\Cref
cor:seq_nexp one can easily obtain that for all
j\in\mathbb{N}
, such that
1\leq j\leq l
, we have that

\displaystyle\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(g^{\prime}_{j},i^{\prime}_{j})\leq\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(g_{j},i_{j})

Using that fact, we can prove the following

\displaystyle d^{k+l,m+n}(f\oplus g,h\oplus i)

\displaystyle=d^{k+l,m+n}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{k},g^{\prime}_{1},\dots,g^{\prime}_{l}\rangle,\langle h_{1},\dots,h_{k},i^{\prime}_{1},\dots,i^{\prime}_{l}\rangle)

\displaystyle=\max\left\{\sup_{1\leq p\leq k}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(f_{p},h_{p})\},\sup_{1\leq j\leq l}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(g^{\prime}_{j},i^{\prime}_{j})\}\right\}

\displaystyle\leq\max\left\{\sup_{1\leq p\leq k}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(f_{p},h_{p})\},\sup_{1\leq j\leq l}\{\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(g_{j},i_{j})\}\right\}

\displaystyle=\max\{d^{k,m}(f,g),d^{l,n}(h,i)\}

∎

Lemma 79
.

The dagger on
\mathsf{RegBeh}
is nonexpansive.

Proof.

Let
f,g\colon n\to p+n
be morphisms in
\mathsf{RefBeh}
. We proceed by induction on
n
. If
n=0
, then
f^{\dagger}=f=0_{p}=g=g^{\dagger}
and hence
d^{0,p}(f^{\dagger},g^{\dagger})\leq d^{0,p}(f,g)
.

If
n=1
, then we have the following

\displaystyle d^{1,p}(f^{\dagger},g^{\dagger})

\displaystyle=\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(\mu v_{p+1}.f,\mu v_{p+1}.g)\leq\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(f,g)

(
\Cref
cor:rec_nexp)

Let
n=n^{\prime}+1
. Recall, that we can represent
f
and
g
in the following way

\displaystyle f=\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}},f_{n^{\prime}+1}\rangle=\langle\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle,f_{n^{\prime}+1}\rangle\qquad g=\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}},f_{g^{\prime}+1}\rangle=\langle\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle,g_{n^{\prime}+1}\rangle\qquad

We can apply the induction hypothesis and obtain the following:

d^{n^{\prime},p+1}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger},\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger})\leq d^{n^{\prime},n^{\prime}+p+1}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle,\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle)

Using it, one can show that:

\displaystyle d^{p+1+n^{\prime},p+1}\left(\langle\mathrm{id}_{p+1},\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{p+1},\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}\rangle\right)

\displaystyle=d^{n^{\prime},p+1}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger},\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger})

\displaystyle\leq d^{n^{\prime},p+1+n^{\prime}}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle,\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle)

For the sake of simplicity, let

k=f_{n^{\prime}+1};\langle\mathrm{id}_{p+1},\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}\rangle
and
l=g_{n^{\prime}+1};\langle\mathrm{id}_{p+1},\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}\rangle
.
Using
\Cref
cor:seq_nexp we know that:

\displaystyle d^{1,p+1}(k,l)

\displaystyle\leq\max\left\{d^{1,p+1}(f_{n^{\prime}+1},g_{n^{\prime}+1}),d^{p+n^{\prime},p+1}\left(\langle\mathrm{id}_{p+1},\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}\rangle,\langle\mathrm{id}_{p+1},\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}\rangle\right)\right\}

\displaystyle\leq\max\{d^{1,p+1}(f_{n^{\prime}+1},g_{n^{\prime}+1}),d^{n^{\prime},p+1+n^{\prime}}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle,\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle)\}

\displaystyle\leq d^{n^{\prime}+1,p+1+n^{\prime}}(f,g)

Because of the above, we can use
\Cref
cor:rec_nexp and obtain:

\displaystyle d^{1,p}(k^{\dagger},l^{\dagger})\leq d^{1,p+1}(k,l)\leq d^{n^{\prime},p+1+n^{\prime}}(f,g)

Recall the
scalar pairing identity
, which states that:

\displaystyle f^{\dagger}=\langle\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger};\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},k^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle,k^{\dagger}\rangle\qquad\text{and}\qquad g^{\dagger}=\langle\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger};\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},l^{\dagger}\rangle\rangle,l^{\dagger}\rangle

We have that

\displaystyle d^{n^{\prime}+1,p}(f^{\dagger},g^{\dagger})

\displaystyle\leq\max\{d^{n^{\prime},p+1}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger};\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},k^{\dagger}\rangle,\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle;\langle\mathrm{id}_{p},l^{\dagger}\rangle),d^{1,p}(k^{\dagger},l^{\dagger})\}

\displaystyle\leq\max\{d^{n^{\prime},1+p}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger},\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}),d^{p+1,p}(\langle id_{p},k^{\dagger}\rangle,\langle id_{p},l^{\dagger}\rangle),d^{1,p}(k^{\dagger},l^{\dagger})

(
\Cref
cor:seq_nexp)

\displaystyle\leq\max\{d^{n^{\prime},p+1}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger},\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle^{\dagger}),d^{1,p}(k^{\dagger},l^{\dagger})

\displaystyle\leq\max\{^{n^{\prime},p+1+n^{\prime}}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle,\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle),d^{1,p}(k^{\dagger},l^{\dagger})\}

(Induction hypothesis)

\displaystyle\leq\max\{^{n^{\prime},p+1+n^{\prime}}(\langle f_{1},\dots,f_{n^{\prime}}\rangle,\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n^{\prime}}\rangle),d^{n^{\prime}+1,p+1+n^{\prime}}(f,g)\}

\displaystyle=d^{n^{\prime}+1,p+1+n^{\prime}}(f,g)

which completes the proof.
∎

Corollary 80
.

The trace on
\mathsf{RegBeh}
is nonexpansive.

Proof.

Immediate consequence of
\Cref
thm:trace,
\Cref
lem:seq_nonexpansive and
\Cref
lem:dagger_nonexpansive.
∎

See
11

Proof.

Follows from
\Cref
lem:seq_nonexpansive,
\Cref
lem:pairs_nonexpansive,
\Cref
lem:tens_nonexpansive,
\Cref
lem:dagger_nonexpansive,
\Cref
cor:trace_nonexpansive.
∎

Every homset
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})((A^{+},A^{-}),(B^{+},B^{-}))
of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
can be equipped with a pseudometric space
d^{A^{+}+B^{-},A^{-}+B^{+}}
associated with the homset
\mathsf{RegBeh}(A^{+}+B^{-},A^{-}+B^{+})
of
\mathsf{RegBeh}
.

Corollary 81
.

The fully faithful functor
N\colon\mathsf{RegBeh}\to\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is an isometry on homsets.

Proof.

Let
f,g\in\mathsf{RegBeh}(m,n)
. From, the definition of
N
, we immediately have that

d^{N(m),N(n)}(N(f),(N(g))=d^{m,n}(f,g)

∎

See
14

Proof.

Immediate consequence of
\Cref
cor:trace_nonexpansive,
\Cref
lem:seq_nonexpansive,
\Cref
lem:tens_nonexpansive and
\Cref
cor:int_isometry.
∎

Appendix D
Soundness

See
15

Proof.

We verify that all equations defining
\mathsf{Syn}
are satisfied. When dealing with left-to-right diagrams, we will make use of the fact that
\mathsf{RegBeh}
fully faithfully embeds into
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
(
\Cref
thm:trace_embeds_int) and hence it suffices to verify the axioms in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
, rather then in their completion to
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
.
(A1)
is satisfied because of the yanking property of trace operation defined on
\mathsf{RegBeh}
, while
(A2)
is its dual in
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
and can be verified similarly.
(B1)
,
(B2)
and
(B3)
are satisfied because
+
defined on
{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\equiv}
is a commutative monoid with
0
being its identity. Similarly,
(B4)
,
(B5)
and
(B6)
are satisfied because of the universal property of coproduct on
\mathsf{RegBeh}
and
\nabla_{1}
being the codiagonal morphism. For
(B8)
we rely on the fact that
\nabla_{1};\langle v_{1}+v_{2}\rangle=\langle v_{1},v_{1}\rangle;\langle v_{1}+v_{2}\rangle=\langle v_{1}+v_{2},v_{1}+v_{2}\rangle
.
(B8)
holds because
\nabla_{1};\langle 0\rangle=\langle v_{1},v_{1}\rangle;\langle 0\rangle=\langle 0,0\rangle
.

(B9)
is satisfied because
+
is idempotent. Finally,
(B10)
corresponds to taking the dagger of
\langle v_{1}+v_{2}\rangle
and captures the identity
\mu v_{2}.(v_{1}+v_{2})=v_{1}
of Milner’s Algebra of Regular Behaviours. Finally,
(C1)
holds, because
\nabla_{1};\langle a.v_{1}\rangle=\langle v_{1},v_{1}\rangle;\langle a.v_{1}\rangle=\langle a.v_{1},a.v_{1}\rangle
.
∎

Lemma 82
.

All the inference rules defining the distance on
\mathsf{Syn}
are satisfied in
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
.

Proof.

For most of the rules, the proof is straightforward. The soundness of
(Top)
follows from the fact that the distance on morphisms of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is
1
-bounded, while
(Max)
captures the transitivity of partial order on the rational numbers.
(Refl)
,
(Sym)
and
(Triang)
are satisfied because the distance function on each hom-set of
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is a pseudometric space.
(Cont)
captures the Cauchy completeness of reals, while
(Seq)
and
(Tens)
are immediate consquence of
\Cref
cor:sem_enriched, stating that
\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is
\mathsf{PMet}
-enriched symmetric monoidal category. For the remaining two rules, we will make use of the fact that the fully faithful embedding
N\colon\mathsf{RegBeh}\to\mathbf{Int}(\mathsf{RegBeh})
is an isometry (
\Cref
cor:embedding_iso), hence for the left-to-right diagrams it suffices to check the rules in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
. The soundness of
(Pref)
is an immediate consequence of
\Cref
cor:prefixing_discounts. Finally,
(Codel)
follows from the uniqueness of maps from the initial object in
\mathsf{RegBeh}
.
∎

See
16

Proof.

Induction on the length of derivation and the usage of
\Cref
lem:soundness_sublemma.
∎

is also derivable.

Proof.

Pick an arbitrary
\varepsilon\in\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}
, such that
\mathcal{H}(d_{F})(A,B)\leq\varepsilon
.
If
A=B=\emptyset
, then by the usage of
(Refl)
and
(Max)
we are done. Similarly, when only one of
A
and
B
is empty, that we can immediately obtain the desired result using
(Top)
and
(Max)
rules. From now on, we can safely assume that
A
and
B
are nonempty. Recall the characterisation of Hausdorff distance from
\Cref
rem:hausdorff_duality. One can easily observe that in the case when
A
and
B
are nonempty, the set
\Gamma(A,B)
of relational couplings between
A
and
B
is nonempty and hence

\mathcal{H}(d_{F})(A,B)=\min\left\{\sup_{(f_{i},f_{k})\in R}d_{F}(f_{i},f_{k})\mid R\in\Gamma(A,B)\right\}\leq\varepsilon

There must exist some optimal coupling
R_{\min}\in\Gamma(A,B)
, which witnesses the above minimum. Hence, we have that
\sup_{(f_{i},f_{k})\in R_{\min}}d_{F}(f_{i},f_{k})\leq\varepsilon
, which in turn implies that
d_{F}(f_{i},f_{k})\leq\varepsilon
for all
(f_{i},f_{k})\in R_{\min}
. Using the assumption, we know that for all pairs
(f_{i},f_{k})\in R_{\min}
, we have that

Corollary 94
.

A function mapping each state
f_{i}\in Q_{d}
to
\left\llbracket{f_{i}}\right\rrbracket
is a prechart homomorphism from
(Q_{d},\beta)
to
\Omega

Proof.

Immediately follows from
\Cref
lem:fixpoint and the definition on transition structure on
{\mathsf{Exp}}/{\sim}
(given by
\Cref
lem:quotient_chart). Essentially, homomorphisms are maps that preserve and reflect prechart transitions
[
43
, Example 2.1]
and
(Q_{d},\beta)
is precisely defined to satisfy this.
∎

Proof.

\Cref
lem:extracted_homom and
\Cref
thm:beh_dist.
∎

is derivable. Since
\varepsilon^{\prime}>\varepsilon
, we have that
\mathsf{bd}_{\overline{\partial}}(\left\llbracket{f_{g}}\right\rrbracket,\left\llbracket{f_{h}}\right\rrbracket)<\varepsilon^{\prime}
. Because of
\Cref
cor:dist-chart-diag and
\Cref
cor:kleene_locally_finite, we have that

\inf_{p\in\mathbb{N}}\left\{\Phi^{(p)}_{\beta}(f_{g},f_{h})\right\}<\varepsilon^{\prime}

We will argue that there exists
p\in\mathbb{N}
, such that
\Phi^{(p)}_{\beta}(f_{g},f_{h})<\varepsilon^{\prime}
. For the sake of an argument, assume that for all
p\in\mathbb{N}
, we have that
\Phi^{(p)}_{\beta}(f_{g},f_{h})\geq\varepsilon^{\prime}
. This would make
\varepsilon^{\prime}
into the lower bound of the
\omega
-cochain
\left\{\Phi^{(p)}_{\beta}(f_{g},f_{h})\right\}_{p\in\mathbb{N}}
and hence
\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq\inf_{p\in\mathbb{N}}\left\{\Phi^{(p)}_{\beta}(f_{g},f_{h})\right\}<\varepsilon^{\prime}
, which leads to contradiction. Combining that argument with
\Cref
lem:approximation allows us to conclude that

Using
\Cref
lem:fundamental, we can show that each of the
\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{m}
subdiagrams is in the form allowing to use

The other bijection is constructed analogously.
∎

Intuitively, Lemma
18
tells us that we can always bend incoming wires to the left and outgoing wires to the right to obtain a
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
diagram from any given diagram.
Let
S(f)\mathrel{:}\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
be the diagram obtained by applying the bijections of Lemma
18
to a diagram
f\mathrel{:}\,v\to w
until all the objects occurring in its domain and codomain are
\blacktriangleright
.

Lemma 95
.

Given two diagrams
f,g\mathrel{:}\,v\to w
,
S(f)=S(g)
iff
f=g
.

Proof.

The idea is that, if
S(f)=S(g)
, we can always show that
f=g
using a similar derivation, by simply applying the transformation of Lemma
18
before using the derivation that
S(f)=S(g)
, and then recover the original orientation of the wires by bending them back into their original place afterwards; and the same idea applies to show that
f=g
implies
S(f)=S(g)
.
∎

See
31

Proof.
